title: In Jensen Huang’s return, unanswered questions of national security, governance and politics
content_html:
President Donald Trump looks on as Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, speaks during an event at the White House in Washington, April 30, 2025. (NYT)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than two weeks after he stepped down as the chief executive of Nvidia amid revelations of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Jensen Huang is back at the helm of the world’s most consequential artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker. His dramatic reinstatement on Monday (November 23) has triggered a euphoric response on Wall Street, but a bipartisan backlash in Washington.

While Huang’s return has brought an end to an unprecedented leadership crisis at Nvidia, several of the questions that precipitated his departure remain unanswered – from the extent of the potential national security risks posed by his relationship to the standards of corporate governance at the chipmaker, and the propriety of the White House’s intervention even as multiple investigations remain underway.

At the heart of the controversy is also a larger tension, as to whether the enormous economic and strategic significance of Nvidia, whose chips underpin much of the global AI industry, has complicated the ability of American institutions to hold its leadership accountable.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Nvidia’s shares rose 31.5% on Monday, adding roughly $950 billion to its market capitalisation. But even as investors celebrated Huang’s return, lawmakers from both the Republican and Democratic parties questioned the circumstances under which the company’s board reversed its earlier decision.

The national security question remains unresolved

Huang’s troubles stemmed from his relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman formerly associated with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has been under scrutiny over the suspected diversion of advanced Nvidia chips to China. US intelligence officials reportedly suspect her of having worked for Chinese intelligence, an allegation Beijing has denied.

The concerns are particularly significant given Washington’s attempts to restrict Beijing’s access to advanced American semiconductors, which can be used for developing sophisticated AI systems and have potential military applications.

Also in Explained | Why Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO

In announcing Huang’s reinstatement, Nvidia’s board said it had received inputs from senior officials in the US government and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. However, it neither identified these officials nor disclosed the nature of the information they had provided.

Story continues below this ad

Crucially, Nvidia said its own investigation, being conducted by a committee of independent directors with the assistance of external legal counsel, would continue. Huang has committed to cooperating with the investigation.

Separately, on the same day that Huang returned, the Trump administration moved to add Megaspeed and several associated entities to its trade blacklist, restricting their access to sensitive American technology.

In a joint statement last week, the US Departments of Justice and Commerce said Nvidia had stopped selling chips to Megaspeed in June 2025. Investigations into the suspected diversion of chips remain underway. No evidence establishing Huang’s personal involvement in espionage or illegal chip shipments has been made public.

The board’s U-turn raises questions of corporate governance

As recently as November 17, Nvidia’s board chairman Harvey Jones had categorically ruled out Huang’s return as CEO, telling investors during the company’s earnings call that the executive’s personal conduct was inconsistent with the chipmaker’s standards and values.

Story continues below this ad

Six days later, the board unanimously voted to reinstate him, saying that following several meetings with Huang, it was satisfied with his forthrightness and ability to lead the company. However, it offered little explanation about how the concerns over his personal conduct had been addressed.

Apart from his relationship with Alice Huang, the Nvidia co-founder reportedly had affairs with two employees of the chipmaker, including Kimberly Powell, its vice president of healthcare, according to Reuters. Huang has publicly acknowledged marital infidelity but has not individually addressed all the reported relationships. He has since also admitted to having affairs with more women than previously reported.

Also Read | What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia and the AI ecosystem

These revelations raise questions separate from those concerning national security, including about workplace power dynamics, potential conflicts of interest and the board’s oversight of its chief executive. They also give a rare insight into how Nvidia operated, and how the cult of power surrounding Huang – paired with the chipmaker’s astronomical rise in fortunes – have effectively made him and the company too big to fail.

Trump’s intervention and questions of conflict of interest

In an extraordinary instance of a sitting US President intervening in the leadership affairs of a publicly listed company, Donald Trump acknowledged on Monday that he had personally persuaded Nvidia’s board to bring Huang back.

Story continues below this ad

“And I convinced them. I made the deal,” Trump told CNBC.

Trump also claimed that US Attorney General Todd Blanche had confirmed that the government did not possess evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang. However, the absence of evidence of criminal wrongdoing does not necessarily address the broader concerns about potential national security vulnerabilities.

There is also a financial dimension to Trump’s intervention. According to a Reuters analysis of his financial disclosures, the President owns Nvidia shares worth between $11 million and $55 million. Monday’s rally could have increased his net worth by as much as $17 million.

The White House has maintained that Trump’s investments were independently managed and that neither the President nor his family could influence investment decisions. Trump’s intervention is particularly also consequential given Huang’s sustained lobbying of the US administration to ease restrictions on the sale of AI chips to China, an important market for Nvidia.

A bipartisan backlash, and more investigations

Story continues below this ad

Huang’s reinstatement has drawn criticism even from within Trump’s Republican Party.

Republican Senator John Curtis questioned which government officials had advised Nvidia’s board, what information they had provided, and how the company had arrived at its assessment while its independent investigation remained incomplete.

“Nvidia’s board says it relied on input from senior US officials to conclude that bringing Jensen Huang back posed no national security risk. I have some questions. Who in our government weighed in? What did they tell the board? And on what basis did the board conclude there was no risk?” Curtis wrote in a social media post on X. “Last week, the board said it didn’t intend to reinstate him. I’d like to know what changed.”

Also Read | What Democrat-controlled US Congress means for AI, trade, immigration, oil

Republican Senators Pete Ricketts and Kevin Cramer also criticised the decision, with the latter arguing that while Nvidia’s board would bear the legal and reputational risks of bringing Huang back, any national security consequences would extend to American citizens and the military.

Story continues below this ad

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision reckless and demanded that the Trump administration explain its role to Congress. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer promised investigations into any wrongdoing by the administration and Nvidia executives.

Separately, California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia to ascertain whether the company or Huang’s actions enabled China to obtain advanced chips or confidential information, and whether the chipmaker misled investors about such risks.

The controversy is unlikely to die down anytime soon, particularly with Democrats set to take control of Congress in January. Huang is scheduled to appear before lawmakers for closed-door questioning on December 1, followed by a public hearing before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3.

title: Mango mix-up: Why Maharashtra and Gujarat farmers are fighting over Hapus tag
content_html:
Alphonso (Hapus) mangos at Pune's Gultekdi Market. (Express file photo: Pavan Khengre)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A dispute over the name Hapus has pitted mango growers in Maharashtra’s Konkan region against those from Gujarat’s Valsad. While Konkan’s Alphonso mangoes received a Geographical Indication (GI) tag in 2018, an application seeking recognition for Valsad Hapus has been opposed by Konkan growers. They fear that letting another region use the name Hapus could weaken the identity and market value they have built over years.

The Geographical Indications Registry had suggested that the two sides explore a settlement, but Konkan’s GI tag holders have rejected a compromise. The final hearing has now concluded, with the decision reserved.

What is the dispute about, and what is at stake?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What does the existing GI tag cover, and why is it important to Konkan?

Alphonso, popularly known as Hapus, is among the best-known mango varieties grown in the Konkan region. In October 2018, after a nearly decade-long effort by growers and the Dr Balasaheb Sawant Konkan Krishi Vidyapeeth, Alphonso mangoes from Ratnagiri, Sindhudurg, Raigad, Thane and Palghar received a GI tag.

A GI tag identifies a product with a particular geographical origin and recognises that its qualities or reputation are linked to that place. It protects the name from being used for products from elsewhere and allows registered growers from the recognised region to market their produce under that identity.

What is Gujarat seeking, and what is its argument?

The application for Valsad Hapus was filed on February 13, 2023, by Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, Gandhinagar, and Navsari Agricultural University. They argue that Valsad and the surrounding region have their own tradition of growing Alphonso mangoes, that the produce has distinctive qualities, and that it should be allowed to use the name Hapus.

In March 2025, the BJP MP from Valsad, Dhaval Patel, wrote to Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal seeking support for the application under the Centre’s One District One Product initiative. He described Valsadi Hapus/Hafus as having “exceptional taste, fragrance, shape, and colour”.

Story continues below this ad

Patel also argued that Valsad and Navsari should have been included when the Konkan GI area was recognised, given their geographical alignment with the coastal Sahyadri region. He pointed to the difference in harvest periods: the Ratnagiri Alphonso season generally ends by the third week of May, when the peak season for Valsadi Hafus begins. A separate tag, he argued, would help Gujarat’s farmers establish their identity and protect them from having their produce sold under another region’s name.

Why are Konkan growers opposing the application?

Their objection is primarily to the use of the name Hapus. Growers say Valsad can seek recognition for its mangoes, but under a different name. They fear that allowing the same name for produce from two regions will confuse consumers and dilute the reputation of Konkan Alphonso.

“The question is not about Gujarat’s mango, but about who will have the right to use the name Hapus. Hapus is only from Konkan and no other region should use it,” said Vilas Sawant, president of the Sindhudurg Fruit Growers Farmers Association. He argued that Konkan’s soil, climate and coastal conditions contribute to the fruit’s taste, aroma and quality.

Amol Bole, a Hapus grower from Shivane Khurd in Ratnagiri’s Rajapur taluka, said Hapus is the identity of the Konkan region and Gujarat’s application must be opposed.

Story continues below this ad

Ratnagiri grower Mangesh Chavan, who also cultivates Alphonso, questioned why Valsad growers insist on using the name Hapus. If their mangoes have such a distinct taste, he argued, they should use their own name instead of the name of Konkan mangoes.

The stakes are economic as well as cultural. According to estimates, Konkan Hapus earns around Rs 200 crore in the domestic market and Rs 80 crore in exports. Growers fear that a second GI using the same name could weaken the premium associated with their produce.

The Maharashtra State Agricultural Marketing Board has also instructed market committees to ensure that mangoes are sold under the name of the state and variety they originate from. It has recommended GI logos, details of registered growers and QR codes to help buyers identify genuine Konkan Hapus.

Political response

The issue has also reached Maharashtra’s political leadership. Industries Minister Uday Samant has said that nobody can replace Konkan Hapus, while Cabinet Minister Nitesh Rane has expressed support for the growers and offered help. Farmers, however, say political assurances must be backed by action before the GI Registry.

Story continues below this ad

Growers are also trying to build a wider campaign. A mango growers’ conference has been announced in Devgad for December 3 to bring farmers and organisations together and decide the next steps. Their demand is that Valsad should seek a distinct tag, as Goa’s mangoes have done with names like Hilario and Mussarad.

title: Why Myanmar’s genocide verdict matters, including for Israel’s case
content_html:
The ICJ in Netherlands ruled that Myanmar committed genocide during its 2016-17 operations in Rakhine State (credit: Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has found that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar “committed genocide” against the Rohingya ethnic group in the country’s northern Rakhine State.

Announced on Thursday (November 19), the verdict makes Myanmar the first sovereign State in history to be directly held responsible for such a crime.

It comes 78 years after the UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, and 82 years after a Polish-Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, coined the term “genocide”.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the relevance of this judgment, and can it have a bearing on other pending ICJ cases — including the one on Israel’s actions in Palestine?

Why holding a ‘State’ responsible for genocide is significant

The 1948 convention defines genocide as killing members of a group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction partially or wholly, imposing measures to prevent births within the group, and forcibly transferring their children to another group.

Also Read | Everyday Global: What is the International Court of Justice

Its adoption marked a unique development for international law governing State actions. In that decade, the most prominent international legal development was the codification of individual criminal responsibility, when Nazi German officials were held responsible after the Second World War (1939-45) for several ‘high crimes’ through a new body of international criminal law.

These laws were codified in the 1945 London Charter for the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, which listed three crimes: Crimes Against Peace, War Crimes, and Crimes Against Humanity. Nonetheless, both the ‘Nuremberg Trials’ as well as its successor ‘Tokyo Tribunal’ prosecuted individuals, and not States, for international crimes, despite the Holocaust being a genocide perpetrated as part of Nazi State policy.

Story continues below this ad

Even as the 1948 convention gave the ICJ jurisdictional authority to consider any State’s breach of the convention as a “crime under international law”, international legal opinion remained that only individuals could be held criminally responsible.

This was clear in the very first of the ‘Nuremberg Principles’: “Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities, and only by punishing individuals who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be enforced”.

Individual criminal responsibility remained unsettled for decades. How could an individual be charged for actions committed under the flag of a sovereign State?

Even when the State of Israel prosecuted Adolf Eichmann in 1961 for the Holocaust, Israeli judges had to draw parallels to the crime of international piracy to make the case that genocide was so grave a crime that any accused could be tried by any legal authority anywhere.

Story continues below this ad

The jurisprudence of such courts, building on the reasoning at Nuremberg and Tokyo, was eventually advanced by other courts across the last century.

Individual criminal responsibility for three crimes in particular — genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — was advanced principally by the International Criminal Tribunals for Rwanda and Yugoslavia, before being codified in the 1998 Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court (which specifically prosecutes individuals).

For the ICJ, States remain outside the scope of criminal responsibility. This has meant that to even hold States guilty of breaching the 1948 convention, the court has historically applied a very strict legal threshold.

History of genocide cases at the ICJ

For the ICJ to conclusively find a breach of the 1948 Genocide Convention, two aspects must be present — actus reus or the physical act, and dolus specialis or the specific intent to commit the crime of genocide.

Story continues below this ad

The road to establishing such intent is especially narrow. Based on the ICJ’s own jurisprudence, “The Court may only establish genocidal intent by inference from circumstantial evidence if it is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence”.

Before Gambia v. Myanmar, the ICJ has ruled on two other cases involving the convention: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007) and Croatia v. Serbia (2015). In the latter, the court did not find the existence of dolus specialis, dismissing both parties’ claims and counterclaims.

Also Read | Explained: The ICJ ruling on the genocide case against Israel for its actions in Gaza

In the former, however, the ICJ did indeed recognise the 1995 Srebrenica Massacre as genocide but held that Serbia’s main violation was failing to prevent individual perpetrators from committing genocide. It did not hold Serbia directly responsible.

Hence, even as the court has held a State responsible for breaching the 1948 convention’s obligations to prevent genocide, it has never held a State directly responsible for the act.

Story continues below this ad

Crucially, in both cases, the ICJ relied on the findings and reasoning already established by the Yugoslavia Tribunal to consider the presence/absence of dolus specialis.

In Gambia v. Myanmar, however, the ICJ’s reasoning was drawn principally from the facts submitted to it relating to this case alone. These included the submissions of the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar and the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar.

Their findings, amidst a vast evidentiary pool, were sufficient to pass the “only reasonable inference” test, allowing the court to hold Myanmar directly responsible for genocide under Article III of the 1948 convention.

Such direct responsibility is different from other crimes under the same Article, such as failing to prevent the commission of genocide (which the court also found Myanmar guilty of). Hence, the court did not dilute its strict legal threshold to establish dolus specialis for genocide.

Story continues below this ad

Implications for South Africa v Israel

The ICJ is not a Court of Record, as understood in the domestic sense for any country’s judicial system. It is not tied to its own past judgments; Article 59 of the ICJ Statute states that its judgments have “no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case.”

The historic nature of the latest judgment itself was achieved through a rare 9-6 split amongst the 15 judges of the Bench, showing continued polarisation of opinion on direct State responsibility.

Collectively, this means that there is no predetermined implication of the 2026 judgment on other active cases relating to the 1948 Genocide Convention, such as South Africa v Israel (2023), in which Israel is accused of directly committing genocide in the Gaza Strip.

Also Read | Why has South Africa taken Israel to the International Court of Justice?

However, the interpretation of evidence considered by the court does have major implications for how similar evidence could influence its future reasoning.

Story continues below this ad

The Myanmar military’s 2017 ‘clearance operations,’ which killed about 10,000 Rohingya people, its brutal killing of over 2,000 children under the age of five, its “large-scale terrain clearance”, and many other such acts were all crucial for the court to determine dolus specialis. Most importantly, the court ruled that the presence of other counter-insurgency objectives during actus reus did not preclude the co-existence of genocidal intent.

In Gaza, Israel has committed similar actions at exponentially larger scales, justifying it as part of its counter-terror campaign against Hamas. For instance, the 2026 UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry into Israeli actions found that “at least 20,179 children” had been killed in Gaza by Israel since December 2023 alone.

The commission maintains that “the essence of childhood has been destroyed” in Gaza by Israeli actions. Notably, in Gambia v Myanmar, the court considered the killing of children in particular to be “foundational” to the intent of destroying a group in part or whole.

This, along with many other such commonalities, will invariably affect the ICJ’s treatment of the Gaza case.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ)
has found
that the Republic of the Union of Myanmar “committed genocide” against the Rohingya ethnic group in the country’s northern Rakhine State.
Announced on Thursday (November 19),
the verdict
makes Myanmar the first sovereign State in history to be directly held responsible for such a crime.
It comes 78 years after the UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, and 82 years after a Polish-Jewish lawyer, Raphael Lemkin, coined the term “genocide”.
Story continues below.
Subscribe to see fewer ads.
What is the relevance of this judgment, and can it have a bearing on other pending ICJ cases — including the one on Israel’s actions in Palestine?
Why holding a ‘State’ responsible for genocide is significant
The 1948 convention defines genocide as killing members of a group, causing them serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about the group’s physical destruction partially or wholly, imposing measures to prevent births within the group, and forcibly transferring their children to another group.
Also Read
|
Everyday Global: What is the International Court of Justice
Its adoption marked a unique development for international law governing State actions. In that decade, the most prominent international legal development was the codification of individual criminal responsibility, when Nazi German officials were held responsible after the Second World War (1939-45) for several ‘high crimes’ through a new body of international criminal law.
These laws were codified in the 1945 London Charter for the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, which listed three crimes: Crimes Against Peace, War Crimes, and Crimes Against Humanity. Nonetheless, both the ‘Nuremberg Trials’ as well as its successor ‘Tokyo Tribunal’ prosecuted individuals, and not States, for international crimes, despite the Holocaust being a genocide perpetrated as part of Nazi State policy.
Story continues below this ad
Even as the 1948 convention gave the ICJ jurisdictional authority to consider any State’s breach of the convention as a “crime under international law”, international legal opinion remained that only individuals could be held criminally responsible.
This was clear in the very first of the ‘Nuremberg Principles’: “Crimes against international law are committed by men, not by abstract entities, and only by punishing individuals who commit such crimes can the provisions of international law be enforced”.
Individual criminal responsibility remained unsettled for decades. How could an individual be charged for actions committed under the flag of a sovereign State?
Even when the State of Israel prosecuted Adolf Eichmann in 1961 for the Holocaust, Israeli judges had to draw parallels to the crime of international piracy to make the case that genocide was so grave a crime that any accused could be tried by any legal authority anywhere.
Story continues below this ad
The jurisprudence of such courts, building on the reasoning at Nuremberg and Tokyo, was eventually advanced by other courts across the last century.
Individual criminal responsibility for three crimes in particular — genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity — was advanced principally by the International Criminal Tribunals for Rwanda and Yugoslavia, before being codified in the 1998 Rome Statute for the International Criminal Court (which specifically prosecutes individuals).
For the ICJ, States remain outside the scope of criminal responsibility. This has meant that to even hold States guilty of breaching the 1948 convention, the court has historically applied a very strict legal threshold.
History of genocide cases at the ICJ
For the ICJ to conclusively find a breach of the 1948 Genocide Convention, two aspects must be present — actus reus or the physical act, and dolus specialis or the specific intent to commit the crime of genocide.
Story continues below this ad
The road to establishing such intent is especially narrow. Based on the ICJ’s own jurisprudence, “The Court may only establish genocidal intent by inference from circumstantial evidence if it is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence”.
Before Gambia v. Myanmar, the ICJ has ruled on two other cases involving the convention: Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (2007) and Croatia v. Serbia (2015). In the latter, the court did not find the existence of dolus specialis, dismissing both parties’ claims and counterclaims.
Also Read
|
Explained: The ICJ ruling on the genocide case against Israel for its actions in Gaza
In the former, however, the ICJ did indeed recognise the 1995 Srebrenica Massacre as genocide but held that Serbia’s main violation was failing to prevent individual perpetrators from committing genocide. It did not hold Serbia directly responsible.
Hence, even as the court has held a State responsible for breaching the 1948 convention’s obligations to prevent genocide, it has never held a State directly responsible for the act.
Story continues below this ad
Crucially, in both cases, the ICJ relied on the findings and reasoning already established by the Yugoslavia Tribunal to consider the presence/absence of dolus specialis.
In Gambia v. Myanmar, however, the ICJ’s reasoning was drawn principally from the facts submitted to it relating to this case alone. These included the submissions of the UN Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar and the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar.
Their findings, amidst a vast evidentiary pool, were sufficient to pass the “only reasonable inference” test, allowing the court to hold Myanmar directly responsible for genocide under Article III of the 1948 convention.
Such direct responsibility is different from other crimes under the same Article, such as failing to prevent the commission of genocide (which the court also found Myanmar guilty of). Hence, the court did not dilute its strict legal threshold to establish dolus specialis for genocide.
Story continues below this ad
Implications for South Africa v Israel
The ICJ is not a Court of Record, as understood in the domestic sense for any country’s judicial system. It is not tied to its own past judgments; Article 59 of the ICJ Statute states that its judgments have “no binding force except between the parties and in respect of that particular case.”
The historic nature of the latest judgment itself was achieved through a rare 9-6 split amongst the 15 judges of the Bench, showing continued polarisation of opinion on direct State responsibility.
Collectively, this means that there is no predetermined implication of the 2026 judgment on other active cases relating to the 1948 Genocide Convention, such as South Africa v Israel (2023), in which Israel is accused of directly committing genocide in the Gaza Strip.
Also Read
|
Why has South Africa taken Israel to the International Court of Justice?
However, the interpretation of evidence considered by the court does have major implications for how similar evidence could influence its future reasoning.
Story continues below this ad
The Myanmar military’s 2017 ‘clearance operations,’ which killed about 10,000 Rohingya people, its brutal killing of over 2,000 children under the age of five, its “large-scale terrain clearance”, and many other such acts were all crucial for the court to determine dolus specialis. Most importantly, the court ruled that the presence of other counter-insurgency objectives during actus reus did not preclude the co-existence of genocidal intent.
In Gaza, Israel has committed similar actions at exponentially larger scales, justifying it as part of its counter-terror campaign against Hamas. For instance, the 2026 UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry into Israeli actions found that “at least 20,179 children” had been killed in Gaza by Israel since December 2023 alone.
The commission maintains that “the essence of childhood has been destroyed” in Gaza by Israeli actions. Notably, in Gambia v Myanmar, the court considered the killing of children in particular to be “foundational” to the intent of destroying a group in part or whole.
This, along with many other such commonalities, will invariably affect the ICJ’s treatment of the Gaza case.

title: NEET-2027: What reforms could be proposed, what more needs to be done
content_html:
The Nandan Nilekani-led high-powered task force must provide a time-bound implementation roadmap that defines institutional responsibilities, resources, technical safeguards, independent oversight, and accountability. Photo: Express
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Recurring controversies over the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) have exposed persistent vulnerabilities in India’s public examination system. The NEET-2024 examination, which saw paper leaks, exam malpractices, and candidates getting abnormal scores, led to the constitution of the Radhakrishnan Committee — whose 101 recommendations pertained to exam reforms.

Yet, the NEET-2026 examination in May was marked by allegations of paper leaks and cancellations, and the subsequent retest (Re-NEET) in June was followed by widespread student protests. Repeated and incorrect questions as well as answer-key discrepancies have further undermined confidence in competitive examinations.

In July 2026, the government constituted a Nandan Nilekani-led High-Powered Task Force (HPTF) to recommend comprehensive reforms in public examinations, including those conducted by the National Testing Agency (NTA). Its initial deadline of October 2026 for submitting its report has been extended to January 2027 after receiving over 50,000 suggestions and extensive stakeholder consultations.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

With no interim report publicly available, NEET-2027 candidates face considerable uncertainty. With computer-based testing (CBT), a secure question vault, last-minute paper assembly, and digital delivery among the reported proposals, we look at what reforms are likely to be considered, their limitations and challenges, and what needs to be done to restore fairness and institutional accountability beyond NEET-2027.

Why have earlier reforms failed to prevent recurring NEET crises?

Following the NEET-2024 controversy, the Dr Radhakrishnan Committee recommended reforms covering examination security, technology, infrastructure and institutional processes.

But the NEET-2026 crisis raises questions about their implementation and oversight. Vulnerabilities exist across the examination chain — from question setting and review to transportation, storage, examination-centre management, and evaluation. Allegations of insider involvement make these particularly serious.

Story continues below this ad
Also read | Under paper leak shadow, NTA looks for spaces for exam centres; seeks AICTE support next year

New recommendations will have little value unless earlier failures are investigated, institutional responsibility is established, and proposed reforms are rigorously piloted.

Is CBT feasible for NEET?

CBT reduces dependence on physical printing, packaging, transportation, and storage, while enabling computerised administration, controlled access, and automated evaluation. But it introduces digital vulnerabilities, system failures, and cybersecurity risks.

A nationwide examination requires adequate centres, secure systems, reliable power and connectivity, trained personnel, and contingency arrangements. Uneven infrastructure and varying computer familiarity among candidates also raise concerns about accessibility and fairness.

CBT’s feasibility must be established through infrastructure assessment, large-scale pilots, and independent technical audits. Changing the examination format alone cannot guarantee security or fairness.

Story continues below this ad

Can a question vault and last-minute digital delivery secure the question paper?

Security must begin with question creation and validation, not merely paper transportation. Question setting, review, syllabus alignment, translation, and answer verification are all potential points of compromise, particularly with concentrated access.

A proposed question vault would maintain a large pool of independently vetted questions. The final paper could be assembled shortly before the examination, encrypted and digitally transmitted to centers, thereby reducing advance access and dependence on physical transport.

Candidates being screened as they arrive at an examination centre for the RE NEET UG exam in Jaipur on June 21, 2026. Photo: Rohit Jain Paras

The question paper repository, selection software, servers, encryption keys, and transmission networks require restricted access, traceable operations, and independent cybersecurity audits. Ultimately, security depends on the entire chain — from question setters and validators to final selection and delivery.

How can fairness be ensured across multiple CBT sessions?

Story continues below this ad

Multiple NEET sessions require different question papers, yet all candidates must compete on a common merit list. Ensuring equivalent difficulty is therefore a major challenge.

Statistical normalisation, potentially using percentile scores, may help compare performance. But its reliability depends on the comparability of the papers and on statistical assumptions. Even small adjustments can affect ranks and admission prospects.

Also read | NEET moving online: Education Ministry prepares CBT upgrade for future exams

Through rigorous pilots and independent validation, NTA must establish that papers have comparable syllabus coverage, difficulty, and discriminatory power. The methodology and its limitations must be transparent and auditable. Normalisation cannot compensate for fundamentally unequal question papers.

Beyond technical reforms, changes to eligibility, examination schedules, sessions, and format could further reduce vulnerabilities. Such changes require advance notification and phased implementation. In the absence of timely official announcements, major structural changes to NEET-2027 should be ruled out.

Can a two-stage NEET examination address normalisation concerns?

Story continues below this ad

A two-stage examination, on the lines of IIT-JEE (Mains and Advanced), is one possible alternative. All eligible candidates would appear in a screening examination (Mains), followed by a final examination for shortlisted candidates (Advanced) based on predefined cut-offs or a specified number of qualifiers. A single-session final examination does not need normalisation.

This model raises questions about shortlisting, eligibility, syllabus, question paper format and difficulty, scoring, and cut-offs. It would increase examination overheads but improve fairness in rankings for top scorers.

Should Class XII marks carry weightage in NEET? Can NEET be conducted twice a year?

On Tuesday (November 17), The Indian Express reported that providing weightage to Class 12 board exam scores in NEET-UG has emerged as a key proposal from several states during “consultative meetings” held so far with the Nilekani-led task force. Another proposal discussed was offering more than one attempt in a year.

Also read | States to Nandan Nilekani task force: Give weightage to Class 12 board exam scores in NEET UG

Weightage to Class XII marks could recognise sustained academic performance, but variations in board examinations and marking standards make equitable weightage difficult. Conducting NEET twice a year could offer candidates another opportunity to improve their scores, but would increase logistical costs and raise concerns about normalisation and admission timelines.

Story continues below this ad

A two-stage NEET, along the lines of IIT-JEE, could address both concerns: Class XII marks could be used in determining eligibility for the second-stage single-session examination.

Could the HPTF recommend changes to eligibility, attempts, or age limits?

With over two million candidates competing for limited medical seats, NEET’s unlimited attempts and the absence of an upper age limit raise questions about the examination’s capacity and the size of the candidate pool. Candidates can appear repeatedly, irrespective of age, even beyond 60.

Age limits and attempt restrictions, common in most competitive examinations, could help narrow the candidate pool.

Story continues below this ad

Can GenAI improve question generation and the quality of examinations?

Conventional software can select pre-vetted questions from a secure vault without GenAI. GenAI could assist in question generation, syllabus mapping, translation, preparing answer options, and calibrating difficulty, creating a larger, more diverse question pool.

Also read | CISF, AI monitoring, security experts: How NTA is changing after NEET leak

AI-generated questions, however, may contain factual errors, ambiguities, incorrect answer keys, syllabus errors, or translation defects. Expert validation is essential; AI may assist question development.

What should the HPTF deliver to restore confidence in public examinations?

Story continues below this ad

The Nilekani-led HPTF must provide a time-bound implementation roadmap that defines institutional responsibilities, resources, technical safeguards, independent oversight, and accountability. Major reforms must undergo large-scale pilots before nationwide implementation.

NTA also needs permanent expertise in examination management, cybersecurity, psychometrics, digital forensics, and vigilance. The HPTF’s success must ultimately be measured by whether examinations become secure, transparent, reliable, and fair. India needs not merely new examination technology but also trustworthy examination standard operating procedures and institutions.

The author is a former computer science professor at IIT Kharagpur, IIT Kanpur, BITS Pilani and JNU, and a former scientist at the Defence Research and Development Organisation and the Department of Science & Technology.

title: Why common infections are becoming harder to treat in India: ICMR scientist explains
Who keeps the internet running, and what happens when they can no longer afford to? An expert explains
content_html:
After the PHP2Shell flaws were disclosed, open-source maintainers helped get security fixes to users, including those on older PHP releases. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

When two critical security flaws in PHP, a programming language used by millions of websites, prompted organisations around the world to take services offline in October, Czech software engineer Ondřej Surý was among the maintainers who helped get the fixes to users.

The flaws, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, led to precautionary shutdowns on October 21 of services run by Japan’s Finance Ministry, US human-resources platform BambooHR, the Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and the Wikimedia Foundation, which operates Wikipedia.

Surý maintains widely used PHP software packages for Debian and Ubuntu, two Linux-based operating systems. He made patched versions available even for older releases of PHP that no longer receive official security updates.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Surý does much of this maintenance alongside his full-time job as Director of DNS Engineering at the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC), which develops software that helps translate website addresses into the numerical addresses computers use to communicate over the internet. He told The Indian Express that ISC had seen a sharp spike in vulnerability reports this year, although relatively few were serious. As AI tools make it easier to identify potential security flaws, assessing and fixing them still requires human expertise.

The experience raises a larger question about the sustainability of open-source software, whose underlying code is freely available for others to use, modify and distribute, and on which much of the internet depends. In an interview with The Indian Express, Surý discusses the PHP2Shell incident, the growing demands of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and why he believes businesses that profit from open-source software must help fund its maintenance. Edited excerpts:

Why does PHP matter to the functioning of the internet, and what made the recent PHP2Shell vulnerabilities particularly serious?

PHP is a programming language mainly used to develop websites. Roughly 70% of the web is powered by PHP. The recently discovered vulnerabilities in PHP were in the most serious category, remote code execution (RCE). In short, an attacker can exploit such a vulnerability to execute a program of their own choosing on a remote machine, potentially gaining full access to the server (the computer running the website or service).

When researchers discover a serious security flaw in widely used software, what happens next? Who develops the fix, who ensures it reaches users, and which parts of this process still depend heavily on human work?

Story continues below this ad

When ethical security researchers discover a serious security flaw, they contact the affected project or organisation privately. Any project or organisation that cares about security should have a mechanism through which researchers can report flaws in its software.

Also in Explained | What is PHP2Shell, and why did it force websites around the world offline?

Fixing the vulnerability is usually no different from fixing any other defect in the software, but the process depends on the size of the project. The work could fall to a single person in a small project or a handful of people in a larger one. They might or might not be employed to do this work.

In the case of PHP, there are a handful of volunteers for whom this is a side project, and very few people are employed directly by the PHP Foundation. Most of the important work still depends on people. As for when and how AI is used, it is important to remember that AI is just a tool that might or might not be useful in specific cases.

How did the early disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affect the release of security updates?

Story continues below this ad

That was unfortunate because people who knew the original release schedule had made plans to properly release the software so that users could upgrade. The premature disclosure accelerated the whole process by a day.

Now, this is the bad part about AI: once details of the upcoming vulnerabilities were known, people started using AI to search for possible security flaws. It was no longer safe to stick to the original schedule because AI, as a tool, is quite good at finding security vulnerabilities, especially when guided by a skilled person.

AI tools are increasingly being used to discover vulnerabilities in software. Have you noticed any change in the number or complexity of vulnerability reports you receive, or in the work required to respond to them?

In my day job, I am the Director of DNS Engineering at ISC, responsible for BIND 9, a widely used open-source DNS server. There was a sharp spike this year in the frequency and depth of the vulnerability reports we received.

Story continues below this ad

Fortunately, after the initial surge, things went back to normal. We still receive occasional security reports, but only very few of them are serious enough to be handled as security vulnerabilities.

That is the thing with AI: it needs to be guided by an expert with domain knowledge. Otherwise, you often end up with serious-sounding reports about ordinary software bugs, or issues that are not even bugs.

Could AI also help maintainers identify security vulnerabilities themselves?

Not only that, maintainers can also use frontier AI models to find security vulnerabilities themselves. That said, both offensive (finding and exploiting vulnerabilities) and defensive (finding and fixing vulnerabilities) uses of AI need to be supervised by an expert. Otherwise, you might end up with a pile of mediocre-quality reports or, worse, AI might miss something serious.

You’ve spoken about the difficulty of sustaining open-source maintenance. Why does so much essential software depend on the work of relatively few people, and what would it take to support them adequately?

Story continues below this ad

When I joined university in 1995, free software was still very new, at least to me, and I found a purpose in making the fruits of my work freely available to others. It was a paradigm change, and I believe many people involved in the free-software movement are still driven by those ideals.

Black October | An expert explains how AI is changing cybersecurity

On the other hand, some people have built multibillion-dollar enterprises on top of open-source software and never even thought about supporting the software that allowed them to make money.

I think we need to find a balance. The free-software model is viable because it gives me and other developers freedom. On the other hand, if many people depend on that software for their livelihoods, we need a sustainable model that allows maintainers to continue working on the software they love without becoming exploited and exhausted.

Who should be responsible for funding the maintenance of open-source software?

Story continues below this ad

That question can easily be turned around: if the people maintaining the open-source software your company uses were to simply walk away, how large would your losses be in the event of a serious security vulnerability like the recent one in PHP? This should give people running businesses the answer to who should fund the work.

Not every open-source project has an organisation, whether for-profit or non-profit, behind it, but some do.

For instance, Software in the Public Interest is a non-profit organisation that provides financial and administrative support to projects such as Debian. Smaller projects can raise funds through platforms such as Open Collective, while PHP development receives funding through the PHP Foundation.

My PHP packaging work can be supported through Freexian’s PHP Long Term Support (PHP LTS) project, which provides maintenance and security updates for older PHP releases, or through GitHub Sponsors, which allows individuals and organisations to fund developers directly.

Story continues below this ad

At my day job, the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) offers paid professional support for open-source projects such as BIND 9 and Kea, among other projects I am closely associated with.

The experience raises a larger question about the sustainability of open-source software, whose underlying code is freely available for others to use, modify and distribute, and on which much of the internet depends. In an interview with
The Indian Express
, Surý discusses the PHP2Shell incident, the growing demands of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery, and why he believes businesses that profit from open-source software must help fund its maintenance. Edited excerpts:
Why does PHP matter to the functioning of the internet, and what made the recent PHP2Shell vulnerabilities particularly serious?
PHP is a programming language mainly used to develop websites. Roughly 70% of the web is powered by PHP. The recently discovered vulnerabilities in PHP were in the most serious category, remote code execution (RCE). In short, an attacker can exploit such a vulnerability to execute a program of their own choosing on a remote machine, potentially gaining full access to the server (the computer running the website or service).
When researchers discover a serious security flaw in widely used software, what happens next? Who develops the fix, who ensures it reaches users, and which parts of this process still depend heavily on human work?
Story continues below this ad
When ethical security researchers discover a serious security flaw, they contact the affected project or organisation privately. Any project or organisation that cares about security should have a mechanism through which researchers can report flaws in its software.
Also in Explained
|
What is PHP2Shell, and why did it force websites around the world offline?
Fixing the vulnerability is usually no different from fixing any other defect in the software, but the process depends on the size of the project. The work could fall to a single person in a small project or a handful of people in a larger one. They might or might not be employed to do this work.
In the case of PHP, there are a handful of volunteers for whom this is a side project, and very few people are employed directly by the PHP Foundation. Most of the important work still depends on people. As for when and how AI is used, it is important to remember that AI is just a tool that might or might not be useful in specific cases.
How did the early disclosure of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities affect the release of security updates?
Story continues below this ad
That was unfortunate because people who knew the original release schedule had made plans to properly release the software so that users could upgrade. The premature disclosure accelerated the whole process by a day.
Now, this is the bad part about AI: once details of the upcoming vulnerabilities were known, people started using AI to search for possible security flaws. It was no longer safe to stick to the original schedule because AI, as a tool, is quite good at finding security vulnerabilities, especially when guided by a skilled person.
AI tools are increasingly being used to discover vulnerabilities in software. Have you noticed any change in the number or complexity of vulnerability reports you receive, or in the work required to respond to them?
In my day job, I am the Director of DNS Engineering at ISC, responsible for BIND 9, a widely used open-source DNS server. There was a sharp spike this year in the frequency and depth of the vulnerability reports we received.
Story continues below this ad
Fortunately, after the initial surge, things went back to normal. We still receive occasional security reports, but only very few of them are serious enough to be handled as security vulnerabilities.
That is the thing with AI: it needs to be guided by an expert with domain knowledge. Otherwise, you often end up with serious-sounding reports about ordinary software bugs, or issues that are not even bugs.
Could AI also help maintainers identify security vulnerabilities themselves?
Not only that, maintainers can also use frontier AI models to find security vulnerabilities themselves. That said, both offensive (finding and exploiting vulnerabilities) and defensive (finding and fixing vulnerabilities) uses of AI need to be supervised by an expert. Otherwise, you might end up with a pile of mediocre-quality reports or, worse, AI might miss something serious.
You’ve spoken about the difficulty of sustaining open-source maintenance. Why does so much essential software depend on the work of relatively few people, and what would it take to support them adequately?
Story continues below this ad
When I joined university in 1995, free software was still very new, at least to me, and I found a purpose in making the fruits of my work freely available to others. It was a paradigm change, and I believe many people involved in the free-software movement are still driven by those ideals.
Black October
|
An expert explains how AI is changing cybersecurity
On the other hand, some people have built multibillion-dollar enterprises on top of open-source software and never even thought about supporting the software that allowed them to make money.
I think we need to find a balance. The free-software model is viable because it gives me and other developers freedom. On the other hand, if many people depend on that software for their livelihoods, we need a sustainable model that allows maintainers to continue working on the software they love without becoming exploited and exhausted.
Who should be responsible for funding the maintenance of open-source software?
Story continues below this ad
That question can easily be turned around: if the people maintaining the open-source software your company uses were to simply walk away, how large would your losses be in the event of a serious security vulnerability like the recent one in PHP? This should give people running businesses the answer to who should fund the work.
Not every open-source project has an organisation, whether for-profit or non-profit, behind it, but some do.
For instance, Software in the Public Interest is a non-profit organisation that provides financial and administrative support to projects such as Debian. Smaller projects can raise funds through platforms such as Open Collective, while PHP development receives funding through the PHP Foundation.
My PHP packaging work can be supported through Freexian’s PHP Long Term Support (PHP LTS) project, which provides maintenance and security updates for older PHP releases, or through GitHub Sponsors, which allows individuals and organisations to fund developers directly.

title: An expert explains why fixing India's air pollution crisis needs more than technical solutions
content_html:
A machine sprays water amid heavy air pollution in New Delhi on November 13. (Express photo by Amit Mehra)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Air pollution is often discussed as if it were primarily a problem of Delhi NCR and winters, but much of India experiences unhealthy air throughout the year, both outdoors and indoors.

North India faces particularly severe outdoor pollution episodes because of numerous emission sources and unfavourable winter meteorology. And every winter, experts are called upon to decode these phenomena — atmospheric scientists explain the meteorology, engineers discuss pollution control, and doctors warn about health impacts.

After over a decade of the problem visibly worsening, it is worth examining how this knowledge has helped understand the situation, the limitations of the current approach, and the kind of information and scientific research that are still required.

The problems and solutions are not particularly mysterious

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The sources of air pollution are known by now — fireworks and agricultural residue burning contribute during specific periods, while solid fuels such as firewood, dung cakes, and even waste are burnt for heating in colder months. Transport, polluting household fuels, waste burning, industry, power plants, and construction contribute year-round. Weather affects how emissions disperse and accumulate; it does not create them.

The major sources of pollution are well established, and we do not need to quantify every source precisely or measure every exposure before acting.

Fundamentally, reducing air pollution requires two clear actions: reducing the number of emitting sources and reducing emissions from those that remain. This means reliable public transport and less dependence on private vehicles, access to clean cooking and heating, viable alternatives to crop residue burning, functioning municipal waste management, and effective industrial regulation.

Stubble burning and firecrackers receive considerable attention during particular periods, but even addressing these requires looking beyond the immediate pollution episode and avoiding purely technological fixes.

Story continues below this ad

Agricultural residue burning cannot be addressed without understanding farming practices, farmers’ economic constraints, and the availability of alternatives. Similarly, reducing pollution from firecrackers requires not only restrictions and enforcement, but also changing social attitudes, with schools, communities, and religious and spiritual leaders playing a role.

Neither problem can be solved by atmospheric scientists or enforcement agencies alone.

The relevance of scientific research

Uncertainties about source contributions, emission inventories, and atmospheric chemistry will always remain, to an extent, and sustained investment in science and monitoring remains essential. Our understanding of air pollution is indeed shaped by what we measure. Monitoring networks, emission inventories, and source apportionment studies help identify pollution sources for targeted policies.

Expert Explains | COP31: What’s at stake at UN climate summit in Antalya

It must also be noted that what we measure in the ambient atmosphere is not necessarily what people breathe. For instance, a rooftop monitor or a model forecast does not tell us the particulate matter levels inside a home while someone cooks with solid fuels. For those households relying on solid fuel for cooking and heating, household air pollution remains a major part of daily exposure. It additionally contributes to outdoor air pollution.

Story continues below this ad

But research should help refine interventions, not become a prerequisite for starting them. We do not need to know the precise contribution of every source before acting on those already identified.

We need greater attention to studying personal exposure, particularly among the most vulnerable sections of society, but these gaps should not obscure what we already know. The solutions we need are often not those for which we lack expertise; they are those that lack institutional attention, political commitment, and sustained investment.

The question of expertise

This brings us to a more fundamental question: who exactly is an air pollution expert? The obvious answers are atmospheric scientists studying aerosols and meteorology, engineers developing pollution controls, doctors treating respiratory disease, and epidemiologists studying long-term health impacts.

Recognition of expertise is also shaped by institutional affiliation. Scholars from IITs and AIIMS may command immediate recognition, while equally valuable knowledge from less prominent institutions and practitioners working on the ground often receives less attention.

Story continues below this ad
Opinion | What the AQI isn’t telling you about air pollution

What about the agricultural economists studying farmers’ incentives, urban planners shaping transport systems, social scientists examining household energy choices and public behaviour, municipal officials responsible for waste management, and public health experts translating scientific evidence into preventive interventions?

Expertise is often recognised most readily when it comes with a technological solution. A new device is visible and presented as innovation, often as a silver bullet for a complex problem. More long-term, institutional and procedural changes, such as improving public transport, managing waste, or ensuring access to clean household energy, are less spectacular. They require sustained funding, institutional capacity, coordination, and often confronting vested interests.

Technological spectacle also raises the question of who scrutinises the claims made by those offering solutions. Every winter, proposals for smog towers, artificial rain, and other interventions are presented with considerable fanfare, despite questions about their effectiveness and scale. Such projects can consume substantial public resources, create lucrative opportunities for entrepreneurs, and offer governments the optics of action without meaningfully reducing emissions.

We need independent scientific scrutiny, as well as journalists, regulators, and civil society willing to question how public money is spent. Expertise must go beyond simply proposing solutions, and involve interrogating them as well.

Story continues below this ad

We should also consider those living and working with the highest pollution exposure: street vendors, construction workers, sanitation workers, farmers, communities alongside industrial facilities, and women who spend hours cooking with polluting fuels. Exposure is often shaped by the work people do and the choices available to them. For someone dependent on daily wages, earning a livelihood may take precedence over concerns about pollution.

Similarly, household cooking is often borne disproportionately by women, whose exposure is rarely reflected in ambient air quality measurements. Effective interventions must therefore consider safer working conditions, viable livelihood alternatives, access to clean household energy, and better economic opportunities.

As an atmospheric scientist, I would argue that we need more science, not less. Understanding the atmosphere, however, is not the same as understanding everything that makes it polluted. We must continue filling knowledge gaps without delaying action on what we already know. The priority must be to translate that knowledge into cleaner transport, energy, waste management, and effective regulation. The real test of expertise is not how spectacular a solution sounds, or how prestigious the institution linked to the expert proposing it is, but whether it helps make the air cleaner for everyone.

Shahzad Gani is an Assistant Professor at the Centre for Atmospheric Sciences, IIT Delhi.

title: Ayodhya to Janakpur: Faith, strategy behind India-Nepal’s new rail link
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepalese counterpart, Balendra Shah, jointly flag off the Saryu-Kamala Express at Hyderabad House in New Delhi on Monday. (ANI Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

During his maiden official visit to India, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah and PM Narendra Modi flagged off a train service between Ayodhya and Janakpur. The new Ayodhya-Janakpur Saryu Kamala Express is the first direct passenger train service connecting the two cities in India and Nepal.

While Ayodhya is revered as the birthplace of Lord Ram, Janakpur, in Nepal, is widely believed to be the region ruled by Goddess Sita’s father, King Janaka.

What is the route of the new train? What is the significance of Janakpur in the Ramayana? What is the strategic dimension to these cultural initiatives? We explain.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What is the route of the Ayodhya-Janakpur Saryu Kamala Express?

The weekly train service will cover approximately 604 km between Ayodhya Cantt in Uttar Pradesh and Janakpur Dham in Nepal, passing through several towns in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

The train’s commercial stoppages include Mankapur, Basti and Gorakhpur in Uttar Pradesh; Narkatiaganj, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Shisho, Madhubani and Jaynagar in Bihar; and Janakpur Dham in Nepal. The journey takes around 19 hours.

The decorated Saryu-Kamala Express inaugural special train, running between Ayodhya in India and Janakpur in Nepal, at the Ayodhya Junction ahead of its flag-off, on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (PTI Photo)

The service will operate once a week, with its originating days being Saturday from Janakpur and Monday from Ayodhya.

The route is expected to benefit pilgrims travelling between the two religious destinations, as well as passengers travelling for business, education and family-related purposes.

Story continues below this ad

Why is Janakpur significant?

Janakpur, located in Nepal’s Madhesh province in the Terai plains, is an important pilgrimage centre for Hindus. It is associated with the ancient kingdom of Mithila, whose king, Janaka, was Sita’s father. Sita is also known as Janaki, after her father.

The city is home to the Janaki Mandir, a prominent temple dedicated to Sita. Built in 1874 according to the Nepal tourism board, the three-storey structure is known for its blend of Mughal and local architectural styles. It is among Nepal’s most important religious landmarks.

The Janki Mandir in Janakpur, Nepal. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Janakpur is associated with the wedding of Ram and Sita. Every year, the occasion is commemorated during Vivah Panchami, a festival that draws pilgrims from India and Nepal. The Vivah Mandap, near the Janaki Mandir, is traditionally identified as the site of their wedding. The city is also known for its many ponds.

Nepal has been keen to promote Janakpur as an important part of the Ramayana circuit, a network of religious destinations associated with the life of Ram. In December 2023, Nepal’s then Ambassador to India, Shankar Prasad Sharma, described Janakpur as an indispensable part of the circuit and said the two countries were working towards establishing a sister-city relationship between Janakpur and Ayodhya.

Story continues below this ad

Where is Sita’s birthplace?

While some believe Sita’s birthplace to be Janakpur, others regard Punaura Dham, near Sitamarhi in Bihar, as the birthplace.

According to the Ramayana tradition, Sita was found by King Janaka while he was ploughing a field. She is believed to have emerged from the earth, which is also why she is referred to as Bhumija (daughter of the earth). The name Sita itself is associated with the furrow made by a plough.

In a 2023 interview with The Indian Express, Acharya Kishore Kunal, former chairman of the Bihar State Board of Religious Trust, cited the Valmiki Ramayana and historical accounts to argue in favour of Punaura Dham. He also noted that the name Janakpuri is a relatively modern one for the ancient Mithilapuri mentioned in the epic.

The region of Mithila was split between India and Nepal after the Anglo-Nepalese war ended with British victory and the treaty of Sugauli in 1816.

Story continues below this ad

What does this new train mean for India-Nepal ties?

The new train is also part of India’s broader effort to strengthen its relationship with Nepal through cultural and religious connections.

India and Nepal share close historical, religious and people-to-people ties. The Ramayana circuit, which includes important pilgrimage destinations in both countries, and the Buddhist circuit are examples of India’s efforts to develop cross-border religious tourism.

There is also a strategic dimension to these initiatives. China has expanded its economic and infrastructure engagement with Nepal over the years. Strengthening cultural and religious links with Nepal can help India reinforce its traditional influence and maintain close ties with its neighbour.

title: How just one ingredient can make ‘fairness’ creams dangerous for health
content_html:
Fairness creams purchased online often lack ingredient labels. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A 17-year-old girl from Keralam developed a kidney disease called membranous nephropathy and was hospitalised after she used a so-called fairness cream with alarmingly high levels of mercury.

Keralam Health Minister K Muraleedharan on Sunday (November 22) ordered stringent action against the sale of illegal cosmetic products and protein powders, as well as those who promote them through social media. He also said that some of these creams were coming from Pakistan. Earlier this month, Madhya Pradesh also cracked down on unauthorised Pakistan-made ‘whitening’ creams.

What happened in this case, what makes such creams potentially harmful, and how does the government regulate them?

The Keralam case

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The girl purchased a fairness cream from an e-commerce platform after a vlogger recommended it. After she complained of swelling on the body (edema), bubbly urine and other symptoms, she was taken to the Aster MIMS Hospital at Areekode in Malappuram.

She was then diagnosed with membranous nephropathy, a medical condition in which the immune system damages the glomeruli, or the tiny filtering units of the kidneys. The resulting injury allows proteins, particularly albumin, to escape into urine.

The patient’s history showed that she has been using a fairness cream, whose samples were tested outside the state and found to have high mercury levels. Several people have since shared similar experiences on social media.

Prevalence in Keralam

According to Dr S Gouri, a nephrologist who diagnosed the girl’s case, the Aster MIMS hospital at Kottakkal (in Malappuram district) alone reported 13 similar cases between 2021 and 2023. The patients had purchased creams over the counter or via online platforms.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | How a fairness cream left a Kerala teenager battling kidney disease

She said nephrologists in the state have been made aware of the issue for the last five years, due to kidney-related ailments caused by high-mercury cosmetics. The issue has also been debated at a state-level conference of nephrologists.

In such cases, recovery may take three months to a year. Dr Gouri said that most patients were young and middle-aged, and none reportedly underwent dialysis. The disease does not turn fatal mainly because of early diagnosis, as the intense symptoms force patients to consult nephrologists.

Why is mercury added to fairness products?

The permitted level of mercury in such cosmetics is 1 ppm, but the mercury content found in this cream’s sample was around 12,500 ppm.

Skin care products sometimes contain mercury, which functions as a lightening agent due to its ability to inhibit melanin production. Melanin is a pigment produced naturally by the body to protect the skin against the sun’s ultraviolet rays, and it results in darker skin and hair colour.

Story continues below this ad
In Express | Toxic beauty: Why Maharashtra FDA’s warning on mercury-laced skin-lightening creams should concern every consumer

Once applied to the skin, mercury inactivates tyrosinase, an enzyme that supports melanin production. Higher tyrosinase activity produces more melanin, resulting in darker skin, while low activity does the reverse. When incorporated in a cream, mercury is easily absorbed into the skin and spreads throughout the body.

According to the US FDA, mercury absorption can cause kidney damage, potentially leading to rapid kidney failure, as well as neurological damage such as tremors, tingling or numbness, headaches, fatigue, and mood or cognitive disturbances.

What rules govern cosmetics in India?

The Union Health Ministry implemented the Cosmetic Rules of 2020 for a separate legal framework for the industry and to protect consumer interests. Cosmetics were earlier under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945.

Section 39 (5) of the Cosmetic Rules fixes the “level of unintentional mercury” in cosmetic products at 1 ppm. For products meant for around the eye, the level should not exceed seventy parts per million (0.007%). The rules also state that product labels should disclose any hazardous or poisonous ingredients, while the inner label must have a statement indicating the exact names and quantities of those ingredients.

Creams purchased online often lack ingredient labels.

Story continues below this ad

title: Rohingya genocide: Why the ICJ’s verdict against Myanmar may never be enforced
content_html:
