Written by Shashank Maheshwari

On November 19, the International Court of Justice found Myanmar had “committed genocide” against the Rohingya ethnic group in the country’s northern Rakhine province. This made Myanmar the first sovereign State to be held directly responsible for such a crime.

The judgment culminated a case initiated by Gambia against Myanmar in 2019. Just two years earlier, Myanmar’s army had carried out “clearance operations” against the Rohingya, and over 730,000 were displaced.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Both Gambia and Myanmar are parties to the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, under which every party is duty-bound to prevent genocide.

The court ordered Myanmar to pass genocide laws and prosecute those responsible, give guarantees against repetition, allow the safe return, restore property, search for the disappeared and provide medical care, and report within two years so that compensation can be decided. The court, however, refused to grant citizenship to the Rohingya.

While the judgment is significant, it remains to be seen whether Myanmar will obey it.

No effective enforcement mechanism

The court’s ruling was based on a rule in the International Law Commission’s (ILC) 2001 Articles on State Responsibility: the wrongdoer must undo the damage as far as possible.

Story continues below this ad

Article 1 creates responsibility for a wrongful act, which the State must stop under Article 30 and pay full reparation under Article 31.

These rules were built slowly and through compromise, even as the idea of holding countries responsible for violating international law has evolved.

Also in Explained | Why Myanmar’s genocide verdict matters, including for Israel’s case

In the early 20th century, powerful nations leveraged these rules against the countries they defeated, with Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles holding Germany and its allies responsible for the losses caused by World War I. International law scholar James Crawford described it as “a war indemnity disguised in legal language.”

An attempt to establish common rules failed at the 1930 Hague Conference because countries feared interference in their political decisions. It was only in 2001 that the ILC finalised the Articles on State Responsibility.

Story continues below this ad

However, objections from countries such as the United Kingdom led to the removal of a proposal to classify serious violations as crimes committed by States. Instead, Articles 40 and 41 required countries to cooperate to end certain serious violations and neither recognise nor support the resulting unlawful situations.

The UN General Assembly merely took note of these Articles in 2001 and deferred their adoption as a treaty in subsequent discussions in 2004, 2007 and 2010.

Thus, several provisions exist and reflect binding customary international law, but no party is assigned to enforce them. The Court admits as much: beyond the measures it ordered, “the choice of additional means must be left to Myanmar”.

The UNSC does not enforce ICJ judgments, even though it can

Story continues below this ad

The UN Charter provides a way to ensure that countries follow the ICJ’s judgments. Under Article 94(1), every UN member must comply with the Court’s judgments in cases involving that country. If a country refuses, Article 94(2) allows the other country involved in the case to approach the UN Security Council, which can recommend or take steps to enforce the judgment.

This provision was introduced when the UN Charter was drafted in 1945, after a proposal by China to grant the Security Council the power to enforce ICJ judgments.

However, the Security Council is not duty-bound to act, and any of its five permanent members can block substantive decisions through their veto power. As a result, even when the ICJ delivers a legally binding judgment, its enforcement can depend on political considerations rather than legal obligations alone.

In Nicaragua v. United States, the US lost a suit initiated by Nicaragua in 1984 over American support for the Contra rebels and mining of Nicaraguan waters. The US discontinued its participation in the case after it lost jurisdiction. In 1986, the court held that the US had broken international law and ordered it to stop and pay reparations, but the US ignored the ruling.

Story continues below this ad

When Nicaragua went to the Security Council, the US vetoed a draft resolution calling for full compliance on 28 October 1986. Nicaragua later withdrew its complaint after a change of government.

To date, the court has not enforced a judgment under Article 94(2).

Also Read | Why SC issued notice to Centre and CJI over appointments of judges

Myanmar, too, could evade enforcement by enlisting an ally’s veto power on the Council. A government that, in the Court’s words, still denies that the harm occurred, and which seized power during the case, is unlikely to write an honest restitution report.

How political compromise has shaped the definition of genocide

The history of international law reveals an uncomfortable truth: even the rules meant to prevent humanity’s worst crimes have been shaped by political interests. When Raphael Lemkin coined the word genocide in 1944, the idea went beyond mass killings. Early UN drafts also covered the destruction of a group’s culture.

Story continues below this ad

But the scope of the term was narrowed during negotiations over the 1948 Genocide Convention. Political groups that were initially included were later removed amid concerns that some countries would refuse to join. The definition also excludes cultural genocide, the systematic destruction of a group’s traditions, language, religion, heritage, and social identity.

As a result of this continued political compromise, the Genocide Convention protects only national, ethnic, racial and religious groups.

Nuremberg worked because the US, USSR, UK and France controlled Germany’s territory, government, and defendants. International law was enforced because these countries wanted it to be enforced.

However, subsequent examples have revealed that international law may be applied where the powerful find it convenient, and attacked, sanctioned, or ignored where they do not.

Story continues below this ad

When Israel captured Adolf Eichmann in Argentina in 1960, the UNSC, by eight votes to none, accepted that the transfer violated Argentina’s sovereignty, and asked Israel to make appropriate reparation. Within weeks, however, Argentina and Israel jointly declared the matter closed, and Eichmann was hanged in 1962.

The International Criminal Court’s 2024 arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu tells the same story. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute. The US responded with an executive order and sanctions on the ICC’s chief prosecutor and four ICC judges, while the US Secretary of State declared that Washington can take actions it deems necessary to protect the US, Israel, and other allies.

The present judgment is an official finding of genocide that grants courts and prosecutors an authoritative record, and supports other States’ duty not to treat the situation as lawful. But its enforcement still depends on whether powerful States choose to act. The ICJ can say what the law is. It cannot make a State follow it.

The author is an Assistant Professor at the Jindal Global Law School (JGLS) in Sonipat, Haryana.

title: Why SC issued notice to Centre and CJI over appointments of judges
content_html:
The Supreme Court last week issued notice to the Union government and the Chief Justice of India (CJI) in a public interest litigation by the NGO Lok Prahari seeking directions to finalise the revised Memorandum of Procedure (MoP) for appointing judges to the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

The plea argues that the revision has remained pending since December 2015, when a Constitution Bench left the task to the Centre after striking down the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC).

Advertisement

Here’s what to know about the case, what the MoP is, and what happened in the 2015 case concerning the NJAC and since then.

What is the case?

A bench of Justices M M Sundresh and P B Varale issued notice to the Centre and to the Supreme Court itself. In its administrative capacity, the court must respond to the plea on MoP and also bring Collegium decisions within the Right to Information (RTI) Act. 

Justice Sundresh, who is a member of the Supreme Court Collegium, first asked the counsel if there were any objections to him hearing the case. Senior Advocate Sanjay Hegde, appearing for the petitioner, told the bench that many judges would be Collegium members and that the objection would always remain, after which the court issued notice. 

Advertisement
Also in Explained | Collegium vs NJAC: What is the renewed debate over appointment of judges?

Earlier, the case had first come up on November 2 before a bench of Justices P S Narasimha and Alok Aradhe. Justice Narasimha recused himself because he had earlier appeared as an Additional Solicitor General in the NJAC proceedings.

What is the Memorandum of Procedure?

The MoP is the document that sets out the steps for the appointment, elevation, and transfer of judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Court. A set of mutually agreed-upon conventions, it was first drawn up on June 30, 1999, following the Second Judges case (1993) and the Third Judges case (1998), in which the Supreme Court gave the Collegium of senior judges primacy in appointments.

The CJI initiates proposals for Supreme Court appointments, while the Chief Justice of a High Court, in consultation with the two senior-most puisne judges, initiates proposals for that High Court. The timeline and the process are laid out in the MoP. As per the Law Ministry’s responses to queries in Parliament, the process of appointment of judges continues to be governed by the 1999 MoP.

What happened in the 2015 NJAC case?

On October 16, 2015, a five-judge Constitution Bench declared the 99th Constitutional Amendment — which sought to establish the NJAC for appointing and transferring judges in India’s higher judiciary — unconstitutional, restoring the Collegium system. The NJAC would comprise a six-member panel comprising the CJI, two senior judges, the Law Minister, and two eminent persons.

In the same order, it listed the case to consider measures for improving the working of the Collegium. The court received suggestions running to about 11,500 pages, which were compiled under four heads: transparency, a Collegium secretariat, eligibility criteria, and complaints.

During the hearings, then Attorney General Mukul Rohatgi submitted that drafting the MoP was an executive function, and pointed to the Second Judges case, which had left the drafting of the MoP to the government in consultation with the CJI. The bench accepted his submission and in its order of December 16, 2015, said the government “may finalise the existing Memorandum of Procedure by supplementing it in consultation with the Chief Justice of India”, and that the CJI would decide based on the unanimous view of the Collegium.

Also read | A lesser evil: Collegium has grave deficiencies, but it compromises structural independence of judiciary less

The order also set out the factors to be taken into account: eligibility criteria such as minimum age; publication of the criteria and procedure on the websites of the courts and the Department of Justice; a procedure for minuting Collegium discussions, including dissenting opinions; a secretariat for the Supreme Court and each High Court; and a mechanism to deal with complaints against candidates. The court described these as “broad suggestions” and did not fix a time limit.

What has happened since?

Until 2017, broad consultations continued between the government and the Supreme Court. Although the fine print of the draft was never made publicly available, it was reported that a draft MoP was first sent to the judiciary in March 2016. It is learnt that the Supreme Court did not yield on two key aspects: that the Centre should have the power to reject a name on grounds of “national security”, and a proposal for a permanent secretariat for the Collegium. 

A parliamentary standing committee chaired by Anand Sharma had said in December 2016 that the lack of consensus between the executive and the judiciary on the MoP was delaying appointments. On July 11, 2017, after the Supreme Court’s judgment in the contempt case against Calcutta High Court judge C S Karnan noted the need to revisit the selection process, the government wrote to the Supreme Court’s Secretary General about improving the draft. However, there was no movement on the MoP. 

In 2023, then Union Law Minister Kiren Rijiju had written to then CJI D Y Chandrachud, suggesting that a search-cum-evaluation committee for Supreme Court judges and High Court Chief Justices include a nominee of the Centre, and that committees for High Court judges include nominees of both the Centre and the state government.

The letter raised questions about whether the government is making a fresh legislative move to replace the collegium system for appointing judges. However, within days, the government, in a written reply to the Rajya Sabha, underlined that it was only a suggestion to act as a “facilitator” and that the Collegium would retain the final decision to recommend judges. 

Once again, the issue was not brought up. 

Also read | Collegium system is better than the NJAC
The Supreme Court has sought responses from the Centre and its Secretary General on a plea seeking finalisation of the revised MoP for appointing judges.

On the secretariat issue, the Supreme Court over the years seems to have accepted the suggestion. The Collegium, through successive CJIs, established a system looking at data and the performance of judges, with continuous logs being maintained. 

On the “national security veto”, although the government has not formally pressed it, there are several instances where the government has, in effect, exercised a veto or simply refused to make an appointment despite the Supreme Court Collegium reiterating its recommendation. For example, in the case of the Collegium’s recommendation that Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal be appointed as judge of the Delhi High Court, the government had enlisted the Research & Analysis Wing to raise questions of his homosexuality and his partner’s Swiss nationality. 

What has the Supreme Court done so far?

In October 2017, a bench of Justices A K Goel and U U Lalit sought the Centre’s response on the delay in a petition by advocate R P Luthra, observing that although no time limit had been fixed, the issue could not remain pending indefinitely. The case was later listed before a bench headed by then CJI Dipak Misra, which recalled that order.

In RTI responses to the petitioner, it is learnt that the MoP as finalised by the Collegium was sent to the government in March 2017 and that the matter was “under consideration”. The Department of Justice (under the Law Ministry) has declined other requests on the ground that the information is classified and under consideration of constitutional authorities. In February 2026, Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Rajya Sabha that “the process to revise the MoP was under consideration and that further steps would follow once it was complete”.

What happens next?

The Centre and the Secretary General of the Supreme Court will file their responses before the matter is heard again.

It is learnt that the Supreme Court did not yield on two key aspects: that the Centre should have the power to reject a name on grounds of “national security”, and a proposal for a permanent secretariat for the Collegium.
A parliamentary standing committee chaired by Anand Sharma had said in December 2016 that the lack of consensus between the executive and the judiciary on the MoP was delaying appointments. On July 11, 2017, after the Supreme Court’s judgment in the contempt case against Calcutta High Court judge C S Karnan noted the need to revisit the selection process, the government wrote to the Supreme Court’s Secretary General about improving the draft. However, there was no movement on the MoP.
In 2023, then Union Law Minister Kiren Rijiju
had written
to then CJI D Y Chandrachud, suggesting that a search-cum-evaluation committee for Supreme Court judges and High Court Chief Justices include a nominee of the Centre, and that committees for High Court judges include nominees of both the Centre and the state government.
The letter raised questions about whether the government is making a fresh legislative move to replace the collegium system for appointing judges. However, within days, the government, in a written reply to the
Rajya Sabha
, underlined that it was only a suggestion to act as a “facilitator” and that the Collegium would retain the final decision to recommend judges.
Once again, the issue was not brought up.
Also read
|
Collegium system is better than the NJAC
The Supreme Court has sought responses from the Centre and its Secretary General on a plea seeking finalisation of the revised MoP for appointing judges.
On the secretariat issue, the Supreme Court over the years seems to have accepted the suggestion. The Collegium, through successive CJIs, established a system looking at data and the performance of judges, with continuous logs being maintained.
On the “national security veto”, although the government has not formally pressed it, there are several instances where the government has, in effect, exercised a veto or simply refused to make an appointment despite the Supreme Court Collegium reiterating its recommendation. For example, in the case of the Collegium’s recommendation that Senior Advocate Saurabh Kirpal be appointed as judge of the Delhi High Court, the government had
enlisted the Research & Analysis Wing to raise questions of his homosexuality and his partner’s Swiss nationality.
What has the Supreme Court done so far?
In October 2017, a bench of Justices A K Goel and U U Lalit sought the Centre’s response on the delay in a petition by advocate R P Luthra, observing that although no time limit had been fixed, the issue could not remain pending indefinitely. The case was later listed before a bench headed by then CJI Dipak Misra, which recalled that order.
In RTI responses to the petitioner, it is learnt that the MoP as finalised by the Collegium was sent to the government in March 2017 and that the matter was “under consideration”. The Department of Justice (under the Law Ministry) has declined other requests on the ground that the information is classified and under consideration of constitutional authorities. In February 2026, Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal told the Rajya Sabha that “the process to revise the MoP was under consideration and that further steps would follow once it was complete”.
What happens next?
The Centre and the Secretary General of the Supreme Court will file their responses before the matter is heard again.

title: Bisleri water case: The chemicals, conflicting safety tests and Reliance angle
content_html:
The Rs 30,000 crore bottled water segment in India is dominated by players like Parle Products’ Bisleri, Coca-Cola’s Kinley, and PepsiCo’s Aquafina.
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

India’s apex food safety regulator, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), on Monday (November 22) announced enforcement action against nine entities — including ‘sanction of prosecution’ for India’s largest bottled water manufacturer, Bisleri.

‘Sanction of prosecution’, under Section 42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, refers to the official approval required from the Commissioner of Food Safety before criminal legal proceedings can be launched against an offender.

The move comes after a fresh round of inspections and compliance verifications. Here is what is known so far.

What is the case against Bisleri?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In a social media post, the FSSAI said that the regulatory sample of “Packaged Drinking Water (other than Mineral Water)” was collected from the premises of M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd. for analysis, and the sample was found “non-compliant with the prescribed bromate limits and declared unsafe under the FSS Act, 2006”.

“Upon appeal by the FBO (Food Business Operator), the sample was referred to the Referral Food Laboratory, which also declared it unsafe due to the detection of polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs). The laboratory findings established violations relating to unsafe food under the FSS Act, 2006. Sanction has been granted to launch prosecution under the FSS Act, 2006, against M/s Bisleri International Pvt. Ltd,” the regulator said.

What risk do bromate and PAHs pose?

According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), the chemical compound is not typically present in natural raw water at high levels; rather, it primarily forms as a disinfection by-product during drinking-water treatment processes.

Exposure to bromate carries several significant health risks, categorised by toxicity and long-term carcinogenic potential.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | The Bisleri scare: What excess chemicals found by FSSAI do to your body

High-dose ingestion causes severe gastrointestinal distress (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea), central nervous system depression, hemolytic anaemia (a disorder involving destruction of red blood cells), and pulmonary edema (excessive fluid in the lungs), according to the WHO.

Further, severe acute poisoning can result in irreversible renal failure and deafness/hearing loss. Animal studies demonstrate that elevated bromate intake leads to severe kidney and liver toxicity, evidenced by marked increases in blood urea nitrogen and liver enzymes, as well as kidney tissue lesions.

Polynuclear Aromatic Hydrocarbons (PAHs) are chemicals that occur naturally in coal, crude oil, and gasoline, and are produced when coal, oil, gas, wood, garbage, and tobacco are burned, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

What has Bisleri argued?

In its statement, the company said, “We are aware of recent media reports that the FSSAI has issued a notice to Bisleri. The matter dates back approximately 14 months, to a batch produced in September 2025 at Bisleri’s Goa manufacturing facility, one of 143 plants in our network.

Story continues below this ad

On September 30, 2025, FSSAI collected six samples from the Goa facility. Initial testing found that five samples met all applicable standards. The sixth recorded a bromate level of 12 micrograms per litre, against the prescribed limit of 10 micrograms per litre.”

Following Bisleri’s appeal dated November 22, 2025, the FSSAI sent that sample to a referral laboratory for retesting. The referral laboratory found bromate levels to be within the prescribed limit and separately flagged PAHs in the sample.

Bisleri said the difference between the two results raised questions and warranted clarification. It arranged for the same sample to be tested independently at an FSSAI-approved laboratory. That test found bromate within the prescribed limit, the company said.

“We submitted the independent test results to FSSAI’s Western Regional Office with a formal letter dated 2 February 2026. We received no further communication from FSSAI after that submission and understood the matter to be closed,” the company said.

Story continues below this ad

“To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI’s website. Drinking water safety is a priority for Bisleri. We maintain stringent quality controls of over 90 tests across our 10-step manufacturing process and will continue to cooperate with FSSAI to address the matter through the appropriate regulatory process. A trusted brand for years, Bisleri remains safe for consumption,” Bisleri said in a statement.

Timing of FSSAI inspection

Bisleri said the enforcement action was announced on Monday, but the issue dates back to last year. As per the company, it did not receive any notices in recent months and considered the “matter closed”.

The sample collection also came amid changes within the sector. It happened days before Reliance Consumer Products, the FMCG unit of Reliance Industries, was set to launch its new packaged water product called Campa Sure in October 2025. Campa Sure’s launch was scheduled just days after the government’s September 22 decision to reduce tax on packaged water to 5% from 18% as part of a broader rate rationalisation plan covering multiple product groups.

Reliance Consumer Products in June 2025 also announced plans to invest up to Rs 8,000 crore over 12-15 months to expand beverage manufacturing. The Rs 30,000 crore bottled water segment in India is dominated by players like Parle Products’ Bisleri, Coca-Cola’s Kinley, and PepsiCo’s Aquafina.

Story continues below this ad

Bisleri reported annual sales of $345.31 million for the year ending March 2025, as per Reuters, and had also launched the product in the UAE last year, saying, “The region offers significant growth opportunities, driven by a large Indian diaspora familiar with our brands.”

title: Why Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO
content_html:
Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO following the board's decision to reinstate him on November 23, 2026. (NYT)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Less than two weeks after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia amid revelations about his extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, the chipmaker’s board has unanimously voted to reinstate him.

Nvidia announced on Monday (November 23) that Huang would return as president, CEO and board member, reversing its earlier refusal to consider his reinstatement despite mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump, Silicon Valley executives and investors.

“Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA,” board chairman Harvey Jones said, adding that his reinstatement was in the best interests of the company’s shareholders, employees, partners and customers.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Trump, who had repeatedly called for Huang’s return, welcomed the reversal on Truth Social. “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” he wrote.

Nvidia shares surged more than 30% in premarket trading following the announcement, according to Reuters. Huang, meanwhile, said he was “honored to return” and thanked the board, employees and supporters for their confidence.

Why did Trump push for Huang’s return?

Despite reportedly being informed twice by his advisers about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy, Trump has publicly expressed his support of the former Nvidia CEO and called him a “legend” in a social media post following his resignation.

The two have had a seemingly symbiotic relationship, with Trump seeing Nvidia as “essentially too big to fail”, according to a November 12 investigation by The New York Times. Nvidia’s success has been integral to the US’s continued position as the market leader in artificial intelligence, a sector central to Trump’s economic agenda.

Story continues below this ad

The NYT also reported that Trump saw Huang as a modern-day Henry Ford who was leading a technological revolution, and that he viewed the company’s fortunes as closely intertwined with those of the US economy and stock market. Trump was concerned that Huang’s removal could trigger an economic downturn.

More Explained | Jensen Huang’s scandal exposes Nvidia’s ‘key-man risk’. What does it mean?

Trump also has a personal financial stake in Nvidia: an analysis of his financial disclosures by The Washington Post found that he held between $13 million and $62 million worth of the chipmaker’s shares as of the end of August.

According to The NYT, Trump even called Huang on November 10, shortly before his resignation, and urged him to keep fighting for his job.

Huang’s friendship with Trump developed during the president’s second term, when Huang and his wife Lori attended a donor dinner at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago residence in April 2025. That month, Nvidia announced plans to produce up to $500 billion worth of AI infrastructure in the US over four years. The White House hailed the announcement as the “Trump effect”, linking it to the Trump’s efforts to revive American manufacturing.

Story continues below this ad

Huang was soon invited to accompany the US President on his visit to West Asia, where major deals involving Nvidia chips were announced.

Huang also successfully lobbied to ease restrictions on advanced American chip sales to China, despite objections from senior administration officials. He argued that wider adoption of US technology would help America maintain its lead over China in AI. The administration subsequently permitted certain Nvidia chip sales to China, drawing criticism over national security risks.

Who else is on Team Huang?

Elon Musk (left) and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the US-Saudi Investment Forum in Washington on November 19, 2025. (Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times)

Elon Musk has warned that Nvidia could lose important business relationships following Huang’s departure.

“Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract,” Musk wrote on X. “Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost.”

Story continues below this ad

Huang himself has spoken about the importance of such relationships. In an interview earlier this year, he said Nvidia had worked with chipmaker TSMC for nearly three decades without a legal contract, with the two companies relying on mutual trust.

Fortnite-maker Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Replit CEO Amjad Masad have also backed Huang’s reinstatement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman called Huang “a personal hero of mine”, but declined to take a position on whether he should return, saying he did not know enough about the matter.

Also in Explained | Behind Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair lies a much bigger China controversy

The campaign has also drawn support from prominent Nvidia investors. In an open letter to the company’s board, Altimeter Capital founder Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker urged directors to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang”.

Why is Nvidia’s board opposed to Huang’s return as CEO?

Huang said last week he would be honoured to return if the board considered it in the best interests of shareholders and employees. However, Nvidia has maintained that he resigned following disclosures of behaviour inconsistent with its code of conduct and standards.

Story continues below this ad

At the company’s earnings call on November 17, chairman Harvey Jones said: “The Nvidia board unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

The company’s independent investigation remains underway, while long-serving CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO.

The board has also established a committee to oversee national security and export-control compliance, as scrutiny grows over Nvidia’s dealings with China. Kress has sought to reassure investors that the company’s relationships with major customers and suppliers remain intact.

The concerns extend beyond corporate governance. On Sunday (November 22), The NYT reported that US intelligence had tracked Alice Huang’s contacts with China’s Ministry of State Security during her relationship with Jensen Huang. US authorities are also investigating whether advanced Nvidia chips obtained by companies connected to her were illegally diverted to China.

Story continues below this ad

The US Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating whether Nvidia’s disclosures misled investors, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The controversy has divided investors over whether Huang’s return would restore confidence or expose the company to further risks. An institutional Nvidia shareholder, speaking anonymously to Reuters, expressed reservations about reinstating him before the investigations concluded, pointing to Apple and Microsoft as examples of companies that continued to prosper after the departure of influential leaders.

The divisions extend to the Trump administration. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent previously called for an outside successor and criticised the Commerce Department’s handling of chip exports to China. On Sunday (November 22), he said the US government was seeking answers about Nvidia’s chip sales to China and who had overseen compliance under Huang’s leadership.

title: ‘Token Factory operates on GPUs procured privately’: Sarvam’s defence amid Chinese AI models row
content_html:
Indian artificial intelligence (AI) startup Sarvam has defended its decision to offer Chinese-developed AI models through its newly launched Token Factory platform, clarifying that the service runs on privately procured computing infrastructure without government subsidies.

This comes amid questions over whether the company’s commercial strategy is at odds with India’s ambitions to build indigenous AI capabilities and reduce its dependence on foreign technologies.

Advertisement

The controversy has brought into focus a fundamental tension in India’s sovereign AI push, in that whether technological sovereignty should mean developing powerful AI models domestically, or ensuring that the infrastructure on which they operate, and the data they process, remain under Indian control, irrespective of where the models originate.

Sarvam’s position is particularly significant because it is among the most prominent startups selected under the government’s Rs 10,370 crore IndiaAI Mission to develop homegrown foundation models. Its decision to offer models from Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba and Z.ai has therefore raised questions about the commercial viability of India’s pursuit of technological self-reliance.

What Sarvam said about Token Factory

In a post on social media platform X, Sarvam co-founder Pratyush Kumar said the IndiaAI Mission, under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), had provided around 20 startups subsidised access to graphics processing units (GPUs), offering a 40% discount on computing costs. He said Sarvam used this support to train its proprietary Sarvam 105B model from scratch, which was completed and open-sourced in February.

Advertisement

“The government did not pay Sarvam directly, instead like with every supported startup, the subsidy went to GPU cloud providers, helping seed AI infra in the country,” he said.

Kumar maintained that Token Factory, which offers several foreign-developed open-weight models, operates on GPUs procured privately by Sarvam, without government support. He also argued that the growing adoption of open-weight AI models globally had created an opportunity for Indian enterprises to access powerful AI systems at lower costs, while retaining greater control over their technology infrastructure.

“Sarvam Token Factory is one of the first large inference offerings in India. We serve multiple open-weight models on GPUs we have privately procured, without any government support. We have optimised datacenter scale inference to make our token cost comparable to or lower than established providers such as Fireworks, Baseten and Together,” Kumar said.

However, Indian businesses often face data residency requirements and need low-latency AI services, making reliance on overseas inference providers challenging.

“Today, India consumes a few trillion tokens a day and imports the majority of them,” Kumar said, arguing that investments in domestic computing infrastructure were essential to reduce this dependence.

Kumar rejected suggestions that offering foreign models conflicted with Sarvam’s long-term objective of developing indigenous AI systems. “Building inference capability does not conflict with our core mission: training our own models,” he said.

He announced an improved version of the company’s proprietary model, Sarvam 105B-1711, which he claimed offers better reasoning, tool-calling and collaborative task capabilities, particularly in Indian languages, at an output cost of Rs 25 per million tokens.

Sarvam also plans to release models for vision, speech and edge AI over the next two weeks, while working with partners to bring advanced computing infrastructure into India.

Acknowledging that developing globally competitive AI systems requires investments running into hundreds of millions, and eventually billions, of dollars, Kumar said Sarvam intended to build a commercially sustainable inference business alongside its indigenous model development efforts.

The strategy underscores the larger challenge confronting India’s sovereign AI ambitions, which is building commercially viable AI businesses today while investing in the expensive, long-term effort of reducing dependence on foreign-developed foundation models.

“We firmly believe that India can and must win across the full-stack of AI,” Kumar said.

What is Sarvam’s Token Factory?

Sarvam’s Token Factory is an AI inference platform that allows businesses to run different AI models using Sarvam’s computing infrastructure located in India.

Inference platforms are services that allow businesses and developers to run AI models without having to purchase expensive computing hardware or manage the infrastructure themselves. While developing and training an AI model requires substantial investment, running it at scale also demands considerable computing resources.

Inference providers offer access to different AI models through application programming interfaces (APIs), typically charging customers based on the number of tokens processed. This allows businesses to choose models suited to specific tasks without being tied to a single developer, while benefiting from economies of scale and optimised computing infrastructure.

title: FPI disclosure relief: Why SEBI wants to ease rules, and could it reduce transparency?
content_html:
SEBI has proposed easing disclosure requirements for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to attract foreign capital, raising questions about transparency and beneficial ownership in Indian markets. (Magnific)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Three years after proposing stringent disclosure norms, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on Friday proposed to make the Indian markets more attractive for foreign investors by scrapping additional disclosure requirements linked to concentration and size.

The regulator said current rules in this regard are more stringent than in competing markets. This means these foreign players won’t now have to report every single detail when holding an Indian company’s shares, but does the proposed relaxation come at the cost of market integrity? Also, the proposed relaxation raises questions about transparency and the ability to identify the ultimate beneficiaries behind large foreign investments.

While SEBI’s objective is to reduce regulatory friction and attract foreign capital, the trade-off could be reduced granular transparency in the case of some of the foreign funds. The challenge for the regulator will be to ensure that easing compliance does not create greater opacity in India’s capital markets or compromise safeguards against money laundering, regulatory circumvention and the concealment of beneficial ownership, market sources said.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

What changes has SEBI proposed to FPI disclosure rules?

A day after SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said it will release a consultation paper to simplify regulatory frameworks for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), the regulator released a paper proposing to scrap detailed disclosure norms for foreign players.

Currently, certain FPIs have to disclose detailed information about all entities invested in them under the additional disclosure framework (ADF), including individual investors, irrespective of the size of their holdings. This granular disclosure applies to foreign funds with more than half of their Indian portfolio in a single corporate group, or to FPIs that, individually or with their investor group, hold more than Rs 50,000 crore worth of Indian equities.

Also in Explained | FPIs pump record $11.3 billion in November: What drove this comeback?

SEBI says these requirements have imposed considerable compliance costs, forcing global funds to undertake extensive investor identification exercises, sometimes establish separate vehicles for Indian investments and repeatedly update disclosures as investors enter or exit pooled funds. Complex structures such as fund-of-funds arrangements have also made compliance particularly difficult.

The regulator now proposes to remove this ADF altogether for FPIs, with an aim to make regulations in the Indian market comparable to other major markets. The regulator has kept the proposal open for public comments till December 11.

Story continues below this ad

Why did SEBI tighten FPI disclosure norms after the Hindenburg-Adani controversy?

The ADF was introduced in August 2023, in the aftermath of the Hindenburg report on the Adani Group. The controversy had raised questions about whether certain offshore FPIs were being used to conceal the true beneficial ownership of shares and potentially circumvent minimum public shareholding requirements.

The Supreme Court-appointed expert committee had subsequently noted that SEBI’s investigation into the ownership of offshore entities investing in Adani stocks faced difficulties in establishing the ultimate ownership of several FPIs. The committee noted that information sought from regulators in foreign jurisdictions had not been forthcoming.

The ADF was brought into effect to prevent opaque offshore corporate structures from escaping Indian authorities after the controversy between US research firm Hindenburg and the Adani Group but exempts FPI categories like foreign government-driven or sovereign funds, foreign public retail funds, and entities listed in foreign markets.

SEBI then dropped allegations that offshore funds had been effectively controlled by Adani and were being used to breach minimum public shareholding norms in four Adani companies.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | Why have gold prices fallen by 25% in nine months, and could they dip further?

This makes SEBI’s latest proposal politically and regulatorily sensitive. The very framework that emerged amid concerns over opacity in offshore shareholding structures is now proposed to be dismantled.

Why does SEBI want to ease disclosure requirements for foreign investors?

According to the regulator, the ADF was more of a compliance burden on foreign investors than a security measure. “Disclosure requirements that are not in line with globally accepted practices could potentially place India at a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis peer jurisdictions with relatively lenient regulatory requirements,” SEBI wrote in its consultation paper.

“Many foreign investors looking to invest in India consider the granular disclosure requirements as an additional compliance burden. Rather than investing in India and being subject to granular disclosures, many investors may instead choose to avoid investing in India,” it added. The regulator also argued that existing provisions like the restrictions under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) and the Press Note 2 issued in March already cover the purpose of the ADF.

“This is positive. It is not going to fully deliver on our expectations, but it is definitely positive. It will widen the participation of FPIs in the market. But actual momentum and flow will depend upon, you know, the relative valuation, the economic growth story, corporate earnings, all that,” said G Chokkalingam, founder of Equinomics Research. “I don’t think this is going to be negative or compromised. You know, it doesn’t stop SEBI from investigating any individual cases,” he said.

Story continues below this ad

The proposal does not mean beneficial ownership disclosures will disappear altogether. FPIs would still be subject to the applicable beneficial ownership identification requirements under the Prevention of Money Laundering Rules. But removing the ADF would eliminate the additional, threshold-triggered, full-look-through disclosure obligation.

Could relaxing FPI disclosure rules reduce market transparency?

FPIs, particularly those operating through multi-layered offshore structures, pooled funds and jurisdictions with limited disclosure, can make it difficult to establish who ultimately controls capital flowing into Indian companies. Removing the additional layer of disclosures could weaken the visibility of ownership chains, especially in cases involving concentrated holdings or large investment positions.

FPIs, particularly those operating through multi-layered offshore structures, pooled funds and jurisdictions with limited disclosure, can make it difficult to establish who ultimately controls capital flowing into Indian companies. Removing the additional layer of disclosures could weaken the visibility of ownership chains, especially in cases involving concentrated holdings or large investment positions, according to market sources.

Also Read | Blue-chip stocks have performed poorly all year. How did they make a comeback?

SEBI had tightened disclosures in 2023 partly because of concerns that opaque offshore investment structures could undermine genuine public shareholding and market transparency. “Now, it argues that the additional disclosure regime is burdensome, internationally out of step and potentially discouraging foreign capital,” said an analyst.

Story continues below this ad

Will easing disclosure norms attract more foreign investment into India?

While FPIs have bought a record $13 billion worth of Indian shares in November, concerns still remain about whether the flows will remain positive if global conditions worsen again, especially after heavy selling in previous months had been a big headwind for the Indian market. Between October 2024 and October 2026, FPIs pulled out more than $ 60 billion from Indian equities, adding pressure on the rupee and markets amid the West Asia war, Ai disruption, high crude prices and interest rate worries.

The relaxed regulations certainly reduce the compliance burden for FPIs, making regulations comparable to major markets like the US and other emerging economies. However, it is only one factor in the grand scheme of things, and foreign flows depend on other factors like geopolitical conditions, earnings growth, and valuations.

title: How India outdid the West in protecting wildlife, and the gaps that remain
content_html:
India now supports the world’s largest populations of wild tigers, at approximately 4,000. (Express file photo: Ashish Kale)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

A cheetah brought from Botswana gave birth to four cubs at Madhya Pradesh’s Kuno National Park recently, taking India’s cheetah population to 62, including 43 born here.

As lead scientist of the cheetah reintroduction programme for 13 years, I found it deeply rewarding to bring cheetahs back to India after 75 years of extinction. The project is just one example of wildlife conservation in India. India has a long conservation ethic, and despite several challenges, we have lost fewer species than many less populated, prosperous countries with more resources and natural habitat.

What has India done right so far, and what challenges remain? When can animal rights activism and human ‘kindness’ interfere with wildlife conservation?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

India’s ancient conservation ethic

India’s biodiversity reflects a distinctive biogeographic history. The subcontinent drifted across the Indian Ocean, evolving endemic life forms, before colliding with Asia about 50 million years ago and received species from Eurasia, Persia and Southeast Asia. Modern humans arrived from Africa about 60,000–70,000 years ago.

Human activities have accelerated extinction rates by an estimated 100–300 times since the Industrial Revolution. Although India faces pressure from major drivers of extinction, such as human population density, habitat conversion, unsustainable hunting and harvesting, livestock grazing, pollution, biological invasions and climate change, we have done comparatively pretty well in conserving species.

Culture and religion shape attitudes towards wildlife. Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism and Sikhism emphasise stewardship of nature, thereby fostering tolerance and coexistence, compared with Western beliefs of dominion over nature.

Although Yellowstone, established in the US in 1872, is celebrated as the world’s first national park, Abhayaranyas (forests without fear) existed in the Mauryan era (300 BCE). Kautilya’s Arthashastra had the world’s first documented policy on wildlife conservation, and the Vedic Aranyakas articulated ethical foundations for protecting nature. Hunting, described in the Ramayana and Mahabharata, was culturally accepted but expected to remain balanced.

Story continues below this ad

This balance was disrupted by successive invasions. Across the British Empire, forests were cleared for farming and timber, often managed for a few commercial species at the expense of biodiversity. Sport hunting and government bounties sped up wildlife decline.

What survived were mostly royal hunting reserves and rugged forests too difficult to farm or log. Many of these later became national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. They weren’t necessarily India’s finest habitats, but they were much of what remained.

Saving the tiger and more

Modern conservation gained momentum in the 1970s under Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. Conservationists and administrators, including Salim Ali, JC Daniel, MK Ranjitsinh, Karan Singh, K Sankhala and Anne Wright, helped shape the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972, and Project Tiger, 1973, which remains the country’s flagship conservation programme.

During the 1980s and 1990s, international trade in tiger parts, elephant ivory and rhino horn flourished, alongside drug and arms trafficking. After tiger populations in China and Southeast Asia were depleted, poachers increasingly targeted India. The local extinction of tigers in Sariska in 2005, despite official estimates of 19 animals, prompted Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to intervene. The Tiger Task Force was formed, and exposed bureaucratic failures, ignored poaching warnings and fraudulent estimates. A scientific assessment found only about 1,400 tigers, far fewer than the reported 3,500.

Story continues below this ad

The Task Force recognised that alienated communities could be drawn into poaching. Implementation of its “Joining the Dots” recommendations, by Prodipto Ghosh and Rajesh Gopal, who steered the science-based policy reforms, led to the National Tiger Conservation Authority, the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, and scientific monitoring of tiger populations, prey and habitats. Core and buffer zoning was strengthened, and financial incentives supported voluntary relocation from core areas. The current Rs 15 lakh per-family package offered forest communities an opportunity for better livelihoods, education and healthcare through relocation.

With 58 tiger reserves, India has secured nearly 70,000 km² of human-free habitat for tigers and other wildlife. As apex predators, tigers act as umbrella species, helping protect entire ecosystems.

India now supports the world’s only population of Asiatic lions, at approximately 1,000. (Express file)

Securing human-free space for biodiversity is especially difficult in a densely populated country. Living alongside high densities of large carnivores also imposes costs through crop damage, livestock predation and risks to human life. India is arguably unique in implementing a model that creates space for biodiversity while offering disadvantaged communities socioeconomic opportunities through voluntary relocation. Regrettably, this flagship component of Project Tiger has not received funding through Ministry allocations since 2021.

India now supports the world’s largest populations of wild tigers (approximately 4,000), Asian elephants (approximately 23,000) and leopards (over 15,000), and the only population of Asiatic lions (approximately 1,000). This is remarkable in a country of 1.4 billion people, many of whom depend on forests for their livelihoods.

Story continues below this ad

Once distributed from Persia to Palamu in Bihar, lions were eliminated across most of their range during the British era; fewer than 50 survived in Junagadh under the Nawab’s protection. Today, about 1,000 share 30,000 km² of Kathiawar coexisting with people and livestock – an exemplary conservation success.

Since the Sariska crisis and reforms that followed, India’s tigers have increased by about 6% a year, recolonising roughly 3,000 km² annually, making India is a global leader in tiger conservation.

What India’s wildlife laws achieved, and what more they need to do

India’s environmental laws were among the world’s most stringent, rightly guarding against short-sighted economic temptations. Mahatma Gandhi’s observation that “the world has enough for everyone’s need, but not enough for everyone’s greed” remains pertinent. Dilution of these laws would lead to compromising protected areas (only 5.4% of total land) for marginal economic gains and risking loss of irreplaceable natural heritage.

Because our protected areas are too small to sustain viable populations independently, fencing them off could have disastrous consequences. Maintaining connectivity through wildlife corridors is essential for movement and genetic exchange; fences should be used judiciously to mitigate conflict.

Story continues below this ad

India has made commendable progress in building wildlife passages across highways and other linear infrastructure. Similar measures are needed in agricultural and pastoral landscapes, where road deaths threaten Indian wolves, caracals, foxes, jungle and desert cats, golden jackals and striped hyenas. Less charismatic than tigers, lions, and cheetahs, these species are no less important to India’s natural heritage.

A pair of the rare wild cat, the Caracal, at Ranthambore National Park. (ranthambhorenationalpark)

Carnivore recovery increases conflict as animals move beyond protected areas. India’s response has largely focused on compensation for human casualties and livestock losses. While compensation reduces resentment, lasting coexistence requires proactive conflict mitigation within communities’ socioeconomic thresholds of tolerance and tangible wildlife-related benefits for forest-dependent communities. This key recommendation of the Tiger Task Force remains inadequately addressed.

Where kindness is misguided

India’s conservation programmes have benefited from government funding across political parties. Yet conservation professionals have not always persuaded decision-makers to act in the “species’ best interest”, emphasised by the Supreme Court in 2013.

India’s 1,000 lions remain a single genetically vulnerable population exposed to catastrophic events such as epidemics. The species’ best interest requires multiple populations across its historical range, spreading the risk of extinction. Instead, we invest in sophisticated lion hospitals. Individual animal welfare is an important ethical benchmark, but interventions motivated solely by individual animal welfare can conflict with conservation. Medical treatment allows carriers of deleterious genes to survive and reproduce, increasing genetic load over generations.

Story continues below this ad

Similarly, failure to control feral dogs and cats due to mis-informed activism facilitates disease transmission, competition for prey and hybridisation with endangered indigenous wolves, jungle, and desert cats. Humane population control of feral animals is essential for wildlife conservation.

A critically endangered Great Indian Bustard at Naliya, Kutch.
(Express photo)

We also fail as technical advisers when policymakers praise investments in zoos as conservation strategies over preserving wilderness, or propose captive-breeding and release of Great Indian Bustards to offset powerline deaths, rather than prioritising underground cabling and installing bird diverters on green energy infrastructures to safeguard the wild population.

There are only two biodiverse Island systems in India (Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar) that abound in endemic biota. Development projects here can have disastrous irreversible impacts on biodiversity and therefore need special scrutiny and evaluation.

The cheetah project

Coming back to the cheetah project, the programme’s larger objective is not simply to establish breeding populations within fenced enclosures; it is to use cheetahs to restore open ecosystems and their ecological processes, as tigers do in forests.

Story continues below this ad

Small fenced populations, even when breeding successfully, cannot achieve this. Four years into the programme, approximately 15 cheetahs are free-ranging, while the remaining 40 are in fenced enclosures, ideally these numbers should have been reversed.

Helping wildlife and humans

A multipronged approach is essential to generate tangible economic profits from coexistence with wildlife.

Community homestays, as in Ladakh’s snow leopard landscapes, should be encouraged over current high-end tourism, with a proportion of all wildlife-tourism profits shared locally.

But tourism alone cannot create habitat or fully offset costs of coexistence. We should also evaluate agroforestry on private lands that creates wildlife habitat, sustainable harvesting of non-timber forest products and their branded marketing, and scientifically regulated sustainable community use of wildlife outside protected areas. These activities already occur, legally and illegally. Legitimising community rights and setting monitored, science-based sustainable limits could support wildlife recovery beyond protected areas and restore balance across shared landscapes.

Story continues below this ad

Yadvendradev V Jhala is Senior Scientist of the Indian National Science Academy based at TIFR – National Centre for Biological Sciences Bengaluru

During the 1980s and 1990s, international trade in tiger parts, elephant ivory and rhino horn flourished, alongside drug and arms trafficking. After tiger populations in China and Southeast Asia were depleted, poachers increasingly targeted India. The local extinction of tigers in Sariska in 2005, despite official estimates of 19 animals, prompted Prime Minister Manmohan Singh to intervene. The Tiger Task Force was formed, and exposed bureaucratic failures, ignored poaching warnings and fraudulent estimates. A scientific assessment found only about 1,400 tigers, far fewer than the reported 3,500.
Story continues below this ad
The Task Force recognised that alienated communities could be drawn into poaching. Implementation of its “Joining the Dots” recommendations, by Prodipto Ghosh and Rajesh Gopal, who steered the science-based policy reforms, led to the National Tiger Conservation Authority, the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, and scientific monitoring of tiger populations, prey and habitats. Core and buffer zoning was strengthened, and financial incentives supported voluntary relocation from core areas. The current Rs 15 lakh per-family package offered forest communities an opportunity for better livelihoods, education and healthcare through relocation.
With 58 tiger reserves, India has secured nearly 70,000 km² of human-free habitat for tigers and other wildlife. As apex predators, tigers act as umbrella species, helping protect entire ecosystems.
India now supports the world’s only population of Asiatic lions, at approximately 1,000. (Express file)
Securing human-free space for biodiversity is especially difficult in a densely populated country. Living alongside high densities of large carnivores also imposes costs through crop damage, livestock predation and risks to human life. India is arguably unique in implementing a model that creates space for biodiversity while offering disadvantaged communities socioeconomic opportunities through voluntary relocation. Regrettably, this flagship component of Project Tiger has not received funding through Ministry allocations since 2021.
India now supports the world’s largest populations of wild tigers (approximately 4,000), Asian elephants (approximately 23,000) and leopards (over 15,000), and the only population of Asiatic lions (approximately 1,000). This is remarkable in a country of 1.4 billion people, many of whom depend on forests for their livelihoods.
Story continues below this ad
Once distributed from Persia to Palamu in Bihar, lions were eliminated across most of their range during the British era; fewer than 50 survived in Junagadh under the Nawab’s protection. Today, about 1,000 share 30,000 km² of Kathiawar coexisting with people and livestock – an exemplary conservation success.
Since the Sariska crisis and reforms that followed, India’s tigers have increased by about 6% a year, recolonising roughly 3,000 km² annually, making India is a global leader in tiger conservation.
What India’s wildlife laws achieved, and what more they need to do
India’s environmental laws were among the world’s most stringent, rightly guarding against short-sighted economic temptations. Mahatma Gandhi’s observation that “the world has enough for everyone’s need, but not enough for everyone’s greed” remains pertinent. Dilution of these laws would lead to compromising protected areas (only 5.4% of total land) for marginal economic gains and risking loss of irreplaceable natural heritage.
Because our protected areas are too small to sustain viable populations independently, fencing them off could have disastrous consequences. Maintaining connectivity through wildlife corridors is essential for movement and genetic exchange; fences should be used judiciously to mitigate conflict.
Story continues below this ad
India has made commendable progress in building wildlife passages across highways and other linear infrastructure. Similar measures are needed in agricultural and pastoral landscapes, where road deaths threaten Indian wolves, caracals, foxes, jungle and desert cats, golden jackals and striped hyenas. Less charismatic than tigers, lions, and cheetahs, these species are no less important to India’s natural heritage.
A pair of the rare wild cat, the Caracal, at Ranthambore National Park. (ranthambhorenationalpark)
Carnivore recovery increases conflict as animals move beyond protected areas. India’s response has largely focused on compensation for human casualties and livestock losses. While compensation reduces resentment, lasting coexistence requires proactive conflict mitigation within communities’ socioeconomic thresholds of tolerance and tangible wildlife-related benefits for forest-dependent communities. This key recommendation of the Tiger Task Force remains inadequately addressed.
Where kindness is misguided
India’s conservation programmes have benefited from government funding across political parties. Yet conservation professionals have not always persuaded decision-makers to act in the “species’ best interest”, emphasised by the Supreme Court in 2013.
India’s 1,000 lions remain a single genetically vulnerable population exposed to catastrophic events such as epidemics. The species’ best interest requires multiple populations across its historical range, spreading the risk of extinction. Instead, we invest in sophisticated lion hospitals. Individual animal welfare is an important ethical benchmark, but interventions motivated solely by individual animal welfare can conflict with conservation. Medical treatment allows carriers of deleterious genes to survive and reproduce, increasing genetic load over generations.
Story continues below this ad
Similarly, failure to control feral dogs and cats due to mis-informed activism facilitates disease transmission, competition for prey and hybridisation with endangered indigenous wolves, jungle, and desert cats. Humane population control of feral animals is essential for wildlife conservation.
A critically endangered Great Indian Bustard at Naliya, Kutch.
(Express photo)
We also fail as technical advisers when policymakers praise investments in zoos as conservation strategies over preserving wilderness, or propose captive-breeding and release of Great Indian Bustards to offset powerline deaths, rather than prioritising underground cabling and installing bird diverters on green energy infrastructures to safeguard the wild population.
There are only two biodiverse Island systems in India (Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar) that abound in endemic biota. Development projects here can have disastrous irreversible impacts on biodiversity and therefore need special scrutiny and evaluation.
The cheetah project
Coming back to the cheetah project, the programme’s larger objective is not simply to establish breeding populations within fenced enclosures; it is to use cheetahs to restore open ecosystems and their ecological processes, as tigers do in forests.
Story continues below this ad
Small fenced populations, even when breeding successfully, cannot achieve this. Four years into the programme, approximately 15 cheetahs are free-ranging, while the remaining 40 are in fenced enclosures, ideally these numbers should have been reversed.
Helping wildlife and humans
A multipronged approach is essential to generate tangible economic profits from coexistence with wildlife.
Community homestays, as in Ladakh’s snow leopard landscapes, should be encouraged over current high-end tourism, with a proportion of all wildlife-tourism profits shared locally.
But tourism alone cannot create habitat or fully offset costs of coexistence. We should also evaluate agroforestry on private lands that creates wildlife habitat, sustainable harvesting of non-timber forest products and their branded marketing, and scientifically regulated sustainable community use of wildlife outside protected areas. These activities already occur, legally and illegally. Legitimising community rights and setting monitored, science-based sustainable limits could support wildlife recovery beyond protected areas and restore balance across shared landscapes.

title: Balendra Shah visits India: What is on the table, from security to AI to cricket
content_html:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah, popularly known as Balen Shah, is in India on his first bilateral visit abroad since taking office in March. He will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi for bilateral talks on Monday, in their first in-person meeting.

Nepal’s Prime Ministers generally make their first visit to India, and quite early in their tenure. Yet, much is unusual about this visit, starting with the PM himself.

Advertisement

‘Nepal first’ PM

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician Balen Shah came to power on the back of massive youth protests, promising a break from Nepal’s old politics of patronage and dependence on regional big powers.

Shah was known for his administrative skills and development work as the Kathmandu Mayor. After taking the top office, in an effort to project difference from the old guard, Shah told ministers and officials to focus on domestic issues. He went so far as to issue a diktat: no foreign visits and no meetings with senior officials and ministers from other countries, unless with a President or a Prime Minister.

Thus, when US envoy for South and Central Asia Sergio Gor visited Kathmandu in April-early May, Shah’s office did not schedule a meeting with him. Around the same time, the visit of India’s Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri to Kathmandu was cancelled as Shah did not agree to a meeting.

Advertisement

Then, Shah said both India and Nepal had encroached on each other’s territory, and sought the involvement of China and UK to address the dispute, something India strongly rejected.

Also in Explained | History of India and Nepal’s border issue

The June visit of Shishir Khanal, Nepal’s Foreign Minister, and Rabi Lamichhane, the chief of Shah’s party, Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), smoothened matters and paved the way for Shah’s visit. His visit is being seen as an acknowledgement in Nepal of the need for continued engagement with India.

The strategic logic for engagement is clear as daylight: India is Nepal’s largest trade, transit and investment partner, Nepal enjoys duty-free access to the Indian market, and India is Nepal’s biggest export destination, receiving about 80% of Nepal’s goods exports. India is also the largest source of foreign investment in Nepal, accounting for almost 1/3rd of the total FDI received by the country.

Thus, even as Shah seeks to differentiate himself from his predecessors, there are key areas of cooperation which India and Nepal will look at.

Key areas of economic cooperation between India and Nepal

Energy: Bilateral cooperation in the power sector has been on an upward trajectory, with developments like the agreement for long term power trade that envisages the import of up to 10,000 MW power from Nepal to India over a period of 10 years. India currently imports about 1200 MW of power from Nepal annually.

Indian entities are involved in the development of several hydropower projects in Nepal, including the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric project under construction.

Energy supplies to Nepal were made more efficient and effective through a cross-border petroleum pipeline commissioned in 2019 between Motihari and Amlekhgunj. Phase-2 of this pipeline has also been implemented. Both sides are now exploring the development of new pipelines and terminals, and Balen Shah’s visit will look into this aspect.

Innovation ecosystem and AI: With Shah representing the youth, the start-up culture is a major area that India is likely to focus on.

Since 2025, several Nepali startups have received training through the India-Nepal Startup Partnership Network (IN-SPAN) in collaboration with IIT Madras and its Incubation Centre Pravartak.

Both sides are working to establish a collaborative framework for advancing Language AI, digital public infrastructure, and inclusive digital ecosystems across India and Nepal.

Education: For the first few decades after Indian independence, a majority of Nepal’s senior leaders were educated at Banaras Hindu University (BHU). But in recent years, Nepal’s youngsters are choosing Australia, Europe, Thailand, Singapore, and Dubai.

Scholarships provided by India for Nepali nationals provide extensive coverage, from school education to the Doctorate level, with 1,500 annual scholarships.

With Shah seen as the voice of the youth, the Indian government and Nepal are looking at the possibility of an IIT campus in Nepal.

Sports: Cricket has found huge enthusiasm among the Nepalese youth. In the past three years, there has been growth in the India-Nepal partnership in sports cooperation, particularly in cricket. In fact, the Nepal Premier League is said to be a huge money spinner, next to India’s IPL.

Tourism: India is the largest source of foreign tourists to Nepal. The data of air arrivals in the last Nepali financial year reflected 311,000 Indian visitors. This does not include the large number of visitors arriving by road. Both sides are thus working to promote shared circuits such as the Ramayana Circuit and the Buddhist Circuit.

The new direct passenger train services between Janakpurdham and Ayodhya, whose trial run was on November 5, will further facilitate religious tourism between India and Nepal.

India and Nepal already enjoy extensive cooperation in culture. Indian pilgrims visit Pashupatinath, Muktinath, Janaki Mandir and Lumbini, while Nepali pilgrims travel to Kashi, the Char Dham, Bodh Gaya and the Kumbh.

India-Nepal border management question

The most challenging issue during the visit is likely to be border management. While India and Nepal have contested some border areas for decades, in 2020, under former prime minister KP Oli, Nepal officially issued a new political map, showing Kalapani, Limpiadhura and Lipulekh in Uttarakhand as its territory. This locks all Nepal’s Prime Ministers in a position they find difficult to walk back from. Also, China has long sought a larger influence in Nepal, including over its boundary issues.

However, despite the differences, India and Nepal enjoy robust ties in defence and security. With the issue of Agniveers being resolved — by giving them a pathway for permanent commission — some misgivings among the Gorkha soldiers have been assuaged. India and Nepal also cooperate closely in areas such as countering narcotics, cross-border crimes, money laundering etc.

Balen Shah’s visit to India will be a key moment for a reset in the relationship. The effort is to bring the ties back on track, with a new PM who has been vocal about not being “pro-India” or “pro-China”, but “pro-Nepal”. The political establishment in Nepal is new and different from what India has dealt with, but their aspirational and ambitious political language is what India speaks, and well understands.
